+ Physical-spatial: Breaking Formation — Score: 88.4
Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The tape on the studio floor made a grid. The mirrors made it impossible to pretend I wasn’t standing in the wrong square. I was on the center line, three meters from the north wall, facing my reflection. Two scholarship kids stood a meter ahead of me, one to each side; two more stood a meter behind them. Five bodies in a shallow V, though nobody called it that. At Han So-yeon’s academy, formations had numbers. I was position three. Back home in the South Bronx, somebody put a speaker on a crate and you found a place to dance where there was room. Here the speaker was mounted in the ceiling, and my place was marked with a white cross. “From the top,” Han said. She stood beside the mirror at its west end, outside our path. Everyone knew her face from television: the choreographer who could turn trainees into idols by taking them apart first. She held a folded hand fan in one hand. I’d learned to fear the sound it made when she snapped it shut. The bass dropped. On one, I planted my left foot and shot my right heel forward, toe lifted. On two, I pulled the right foot back beneath me and popped my chest. On three, I stepped half a meter right. On four, my left foot closed beside it, ankles nearly touching. All five of us had shifted east together. So far, fine. Street dancers could count. It was what happened between the numbers that got me. On five, we stepped left toward the mirror. On six, right: a full meter forward between the two steps. The pair ahead of me moved toward the glass; I moved into the space they had left; the pair behind moved into mine. Nobody touched. On seven, we pivoted a quarter turn clockwise on the right foot to face the east wall. On eight, the left foot slid in, both elbows struck outward at shoulder height, and every chin snapped level. In the mirror, which now caught us sideways, my elbow finished a breath late. *Snap.* The music cut. Han hadn’t touched the controls; an assistant by the west wall had. “Position three,” she said. She rarely used my name. “Your chest moves on one-and-two.” “That’s where the groove is.” “The chest moves on two.” The other dancers kept their elbows up while she spoke. I lowered mine, then saw them and lifted them again. Even resting here had rules I couldn’t catch fast enough. At home, a heel-toe opened into whatever the track offered. I could let my shoulders lag, drop into a bounce, change direction if a friend cut across the circle. I had won this scholarship with a freestyle like that. Han had watched from the back of the audition room, her face unreadable. Now she walked toward me across the empty strip between our V and the mirror. “You hear the music,” she said. “I saw that. But when you answer it, you leave four people waiting.” Up close, her fan was black lacquer, its ribs shining. My sneakers had a split seam near the little toe. Tuition was covered; shoes weren’t. My mother had sent me here with grocery money folded inside my sock, and I’d spent my first week pretending I knew which fork to take from the dining-hall tray. When my classmates traded trainee stories in fast Korean, I caught the punch lines too late. I could usually make my body speak before my mouth had to. In this room, even that came out wrong. Han returned to the west edge of the mirror. We walked back to our crosses, reversing the route: I stepped a meter away from the glass, then half a meter left, until the center line was under my shoes again. “Again.” Heel. Chest. Right. Close. The track had a little scratch under count four. My left knee softened to catch it. Muscle memory took the invitation: my weight rolled across the balls of my feet, my shoulder followed, and the close became the beginning of a top rock. By five, my left foot was crossing in front of my right instead of traveling straight toward the mirror. I uncrossed on six and pushed forward, but I’d lost half a beat. The front pair reached their new marks; I came up behind the gap between them. *Snap.* Han looked at my feet, then at the strip of floor I should have covered. “You can do it,” she said. That was worse than being told I couldn’t. “You choose not to.” I stared at my white cross. I had spent years learning not to dance like anyone else. Here, every reflection was meant to match its neighbor. If I finally learned to fit, would I still know when the music was asking me to turn? We reset. The dancer ahead and left of me, Minji, gave my reflection the smallest nod before facing front again. Not encouragement exactly. More like: *We need you here.* The beat started. On one, I sent my right heel out and kept my weight over the left. The bass wanted my ribs; I held them still until two, then hit the chest pop clean. Right on three. Left closed on four. My body begged to ride that scratch, to let a shoulder loosen and pull the rest of me after it. I could flatten everything. Han would get her eight counts. Or I could give the sound an answer without making Minji wait for me. Between four and five, while both feet were planted, I let a small wave pass through my spine. It began below the ribs and ended before my shoulders moved. On five my left foot went straight north; on six my right followed. I was exactly one meter closer to the mirror. We turned east together on seven. On eight, my left foot sealed the stance and my elbows struck level with four others. The fan snapped shut. Nobody moved. Han came close enough to see the white cross now behind my heels. “I didn’t give you that wave,” she said. “No.” She studied me, then the straight line of our five shoulders in the mirror. “It didn’t make you late.” “No.” Her fan opened with a soft rush. “Again,” she said. “Keep the marks.” We walked back to our crosses. I didn’t know whether I’d been allowed to keep the wave. I only knew where my feet had to land, and that I could still feel it moving between them.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional technical mastery in fulfilling the prompt's demanding requirements. The author maintains meticulous spatial tracking throughout, creating a vivid kinetic map where every movement, position, and formation shift is precisely rendered. The grid system, marked crosses, and directional references (north wall, east wall, center line) establish clear spatial coordinates that never waver. The contrast between street and commercial dance styles is expertly woven through both physical description and internal conflict. Technical terminology feels authentic without being ostentatious - "top rock," "heel-toe," "freestyle" from street culture clash naturally with the numbered formations and militaristic precision of K-pop training. The protagonist's muscle memory betrayals are particularly well-executed, showing rather than telling the cultural collision. The narrative voice maintains consistent authenticity throughout - a street dancer's perspective that's observant, slightly defensive, but not overly articulate in ways that would betray the character. The internal monologue effectively captures culture shock and class anxiety without becoming heavy-handed. Details like the split sneaker seam and grocery money in the sock efficiently establish economic disparity. Han So-yeon emerges as a formidable antagonist through minimal but precise characterization. Her fan becomes an effective symbol of authority, and her dialogue reveals calculated psychological pressure. The power dynamic feels genuine and threatening without melodrama. The piece's structure builds tension effectively toward the crucial decision point. The protagonist's choice to incorporate the spine wave while maintaining formation marks represents a sophisticated middle path - neither complete conformity nor outright rebellion. This resolution feels earned rather than convenient. The writing demonstrates remarkable restraint, avoiding purple prose while maintaining rich sensory detail. Sentences flow with natural rhythm that mirrors the dance movements being described. The piece succeeds in making the reader feel the physical constraints and possibilities of the studio space. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the technical precision slightly overshadows emotional resonance, and the ending, while well-crafted, could have pushed the internal conflict slightly deeper. However, these are minor critiques of an otherwise accomplished piece that fully delivers on an exceptionally challenging prompt. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 81.8
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
“ALL RISE,” said the bailiff. His voice made the stone benches rise with the people. A clerk hurriedly pushed them back down. Dream entered the Court of the Dreaming and took his seat. He glanced at the docket. For a moment, his expression changed by no more than the narrowing of one eye. “Territorial dispute,” he said. “Over a field.” “Of wildflowers, my lord,” said the clerk. “I had gathered.” The petitioner stood beside a table piled with sketches. First Love was rosy-cheeked, dressed for a wedding she had not been invited to, and worrying the edge of a ribbon between her fingers. Across the aisle, Mora lounged with her boots on counsel’s table. The bailiff stared at them until she put them down. They left no marks on the wood, but the clerk wrote down *damage to court property* anyway. “The dream belongs to Max,” First Love said. “I made it for him.” “You can see the difficulty already,” Dream murmured. “He is fourteen. He has been dreaming it every Thursday for six weeks. He lies in a field beside a girl from school. They talk about nothing important. She rolls over to steal the flower he’s holding, they nearly kiss, and he wakes with the agreeable impression that something momentous might happen tomorrow.” First Love laid out her sketches. Each showed the same field with tiny adjustments to the light, the distance between two hands, or the placement of a beetle. “The beetle was essential,” she said. “It gave him somewhere to look when he got shy.” Dream studied the drawings. “And the girl?” “Lena. Max likes her.” “Does Lena know?” “Not outside the dream.” “Then proceed carefully.” First Love’s cheeks deepened. “Of course, my lord.” “Then Mora entered,” said the clerk. “I was passing through,” Mora said. “You entered it eleven times.” “I pass through slowly.” First Love pulled a final sketch from beneath the others. In it, Lena had rolled across the grass to pin Max in a game of keep-away. Her face had begun to change. Its familiar prettiness remained, which seemed to make the other features worse: the hollow eyes, the jaw opening too far, the hair drifting upward like smoke. The figure sat on Max’s chest while the flowers folded shut around them. “He couldn’t move,” First Love said. “She took his breath. Now he’s afraid to go to sleep on Thursdays.” Mora spread her hands. “A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” The clerk recorded this as *respondent cites necessity*. Dream looked at Mora. “You have your own territory.” “It’s crowded. Half the sleepers wake up the moment I settle in. The other half have learned to call it sleep paralysis and wait me out.” She sounded personally wounded by the phrase. “Max stayed.” “Because he trusted the dream,” First Love said. Mora gave her a level look. “Yes. That helped.” The ribbon snapped in First Love’s hands. Dream turned a page of the docket. “Witness.” The bailiff struck the floor with his staff. “LET LEE-NAR VOSS APPROACH.” A figure appeared at the witness rail: a dream-copy of Lena, made from Max’s memory. She wore a school cardigan and had a daisy tucked behind one ear. At the sound of the bailiff’s voice, she flinched. “My name is Lena,” she said. “LEE-NAR VOSS,” the bailiff repeated, more ominously. “Enough,” said Dream. Lena took the oath, which the clerk assured her would expire when the hearing ended. “What happened?” Dream asked. “We were talking,” she said. “Max told me the beetle was going to law school.” “It was a joke,” First Love said quickly. “It was quite good.” Lena looked toward the sketch. “I tried to take his flower. Then I wasn’t there anymore. I could see him, but I couldn’t make my hands work.” First Love went pale. Mora examined her nails. “So,” Dream said, “you took the girl’s place as well as the field.” “Only for the end.” “The end is generally when he remembers it.” Mora opened her mouth, then closed it. The bailiff struck the floor again. “SUMMON MACKS.” A boy appeared at the rail in his pajamas, looking deeply offended to find himself in a courtroom while asleep. “It’s Max,” he said. “MACKS,” boomed the bailiff. Max looked to Dream. “Do I get a lawyer?” “No,” Dream said. “You get to answer one question. Which dream would you like to have?” Max glanced at the two entities. First Love smiled with painful encouragement. Mora did not smile at all. “The old one,” he said. “I think. Only, could it stop right before we nearly kiss? It’s done that six times.” First Love made a small, stricken noise. “The uncertainty is the point.” “I know,” Max said. “It’s getting predictable.” Dream rested his chin on one hand. His fingers tapped the arm of his chair once. “An expertly maintained disappointment,” he said. “That is not what I—” First Love began. “And as for the new version?” Dream asked Max. “I hate it.” Max hesitated. “I know it isn’t really Lena. But when I see her at school, I remember her sitting on me, and then I can’t talk properly.” Mora’s gaze dropped to the table. For the first time since entering court, she had nothing practical to say. Dream dismissed the witnesses. Max vanished first, back to the untroubled portion of his sleep. Lena’s copy lingered just long enough to take the daisy from her hair and leave it on the rail. “The ruling,” Dream said. “Neither of you owns Max’s dream. First Love may tend the field, provided she permits the boy an ending she has not already drawn. Mora will not enter it again, or borrow Lena’s face elsewhere.” Mora lifted a hand. “My lord, with respect—” “You require food. I have not forgotten.” That faint movement returned to Dream’s fingers. He looked at the clerk, then at the towering stack of petitions beside her: disputes over staircases, missing teeth, and whether a recurring examination could legally include a second paper. “Mora may feed on dread produced by this court’s administrative process,” he said. The clerk stared at him. “All of it?” “Begin with her own license application.” A blank form appeared before Mora. It was twelve pages long. At the bottom of the first page, in small print, it requested details of every dream she had entered without permission. Mora picked it up. A little of the color went out of her face. Dream rose. His expression was once again unreadable, except for the briefest glance at the form. “Court adjourned.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt's requirements, successfully creating a courtroom scene in the Dreaming that balances dark fantasy with understated comedy. The author captures Dream's characteristic voice well - aloof, slightly irritated, and prone to subtle mischief, as evidenced in his final punishment for Mora involving bureaucratic paperwork. The characterizations are particularly effective. First Love is portrayed with appropriate earnestness and slight naivety, while Mora's pragmatic "a girl's gotta eat" defense creates genuine humor without undermining the darker elements. The witnesses Max and Lena feel authentic in their responses, especially Max's complaint about the predictable "almost-kiss" and Lena's confusion at being displaced from her own dream-role. The dialogue carries the piece effectively, with each character having a distinct voice. Dream's dry observations ("An expertly maintained disappointment") and the bailiff's booming mispronunciations of names add layers of humor. The courtroom procedural elements blend seamlessly with the fantastical setting. The prose is clean and economical, following the instruction to use descriptives sparingly. The author shows restraint in world-building, letting the dialogue and action carry the scene rather than over-explaining the dream court's mechanics. The pacing moves briskly through the proceedings without feeling rushed. The resolution demonstrates Dream's characteristic mixture of justice and subtle cruelty - solving the immediate problem while creating a new torment for Mora through bureaucracy. This feels earned and consistent with the character while providing a satisfying conclusion that addresses all parties' concerns. The dark comedy emerges naturally from the situation rather than being forced, particularly in moments like the clerk writing down "damage to court property" for invisible boot marks, or Mora's growing horror at the twelve-page form. The piece maintains its tone throughout without veering into either excessive darkness or inappropriate lightness. Minor weaknesses include some moments where the humor could be sharper, and occasionally the dialogue feels slightly exposition-heavy, though this serves the courtroom setting reasonably well. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 80.0
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Blood Moon The wolves begin howling before the moon turns red. Their cries come from the forest beyond Saint Wenceslas’s abbey, never quite together: one long note, a silence, then two short ones from farther off. Yennefer pauses beneath the gatehouse arch to listen. The abbey’s chapel bell answers with a single, low stroke. It is midnight. No one stands in the bell tower. “Subtle,” she says. A man steps from the shadows beside the stables. His coat is red, his hat broad-brimmed, his spectacles orange. In each hand he carries a pistol larger than any firearm this century has yet imagined. Yennefer raises two fingers. He smiles, showing his teeth. “You saw me.” “I smelled the grave.” “And I smelled lilac and gooseberries.” His gaze moves to her raised hand. “What happens if you finish that gesture?” “You discover whether you can survive it.” The Hellsing Organization’s mirror has brought Alucard to fourteenth-century Bohemia with instructions to destroy the creatures gathering here. It has neglected to mention a sorceress. He hopes she is not an oversight. The chapel bell sounds again. This time, someone screams inside. Yennefer reaches the chapel doors first, though Alucard leaves the stables first. He watches the violet flare of her portal collapse behind her as she shoves the doors open. Within, six villagers kneel in the pews. Their wrists are tied. At the altar stands a pale priest holding a little girl by the shoulder. Under the blood-red light of the windows, his shadow writhes independently of him. “Father Matěj,” Yennefer says. “Let her go.” The priest’s eyes settle on Alucard. “You’ve brought another of us.” Alucard fires. The silver bullet tears through Matěj’s throat and strikes the stone beyond. The priest falls. The girl breaks free, but before she reaches the aisle, Matěj sits up, pressing a hand to the wound. “Not very much like me,” Alucard says. Matěj’s shadow rises from the floor and becomes three gaunt figures. They rush him. Alucard lets the first sink its teeth into his neck before shooting it through the skull. The second he catches by the jaw. Its head comes away in his hand. Yennefer throws up a shield between the third figure and the villagers. It strikes the barrier, claws screeching against violet light. She closes her fist, and it burns to ash. For an instant Alucard looks at her rather than his own healing neck. The interest in his face is unmistakable. She dislikes it. She dislikes even more that she feels some in return. Outside, the wolves howl—three voices, then one. “You promised me a bargain,” Yennefer tells Matěj. “I promised you the truth.” The priest pushes himself upright. “The bell can return what the body has lost. Even a change made by magic.” She has spent centuries learning which promises conceal a trick. This one conceals a temptation. The bronze above them hums in answer to Matěj’s voice, and she feels its power reach toward the old alterations in her flesh. “It requires a death,” she says. “One life, for what was taken from another.” Matěj tightens his grip on the altar rail. “I intend to be human again.” “You could have asked the girl to stand beneath it,” Alucard says. “Instead you tied up witnesses.” “I am not a monster.” Alucard’s grin disappears. “Then stop feeding like one.” Matěj lunges for the bell rope. Yennefer catches his wrist with a binding spell, but his shadow slips free and seizes the rope instead. The bell rings. Above their heads, the tower stones begin to split. The villagers cry out as thin red lines of light form beneath their feet, converging on the little girl. Matěj has chosen her after all. Yennefer pulls the child toward her. The lines follow. “The bell has named her,” Matěj says. Blood bubbles through his smile. “You cannot change its mind.” “I can change its target.” Alucard glances up at the bell, then at her. “Can you?” “Yes.” She sees no reason to soften the rest. “Once it takes your life, I have to break it before it takes the next.” Matěj laughs. “He has more than one.” Alucard’s shadow spreads across the chapel floor. Eyes open inside it, too many to count. Yennefer sees the lives bound to him, and for a moment revulsion nearly breaks her concentration. “You might all die,” she tells him. “I heard.” “And you’re smiling.” “I haven’t decided whether that means I trust you.” The red lines draw tighter around the girl’s shoes. Yennefer steps between her and the altar, catches Alucard’s outstretched hand, and drives her spell through him. He could resist. She feels the force gathered in him, vast and impatient. He lets her move him beneath the tower. The bell strikes a third time. Alucard falls without a sound. Matěj tears free of Yennefer’s weakened binding and rushes at the child. She flings him across the chapel, but the effort costs her: the bell begins to swing again, and red light spills over Alucard’s body. She could hold Matěj until dawn. She could leave the bell intact and learn everything it knows. For one treacherous heartbeat she hears, beneath its tolling, the promise it made her. Then the little girl takes her hand. Yennefer sends every thread of magic she has into the tower. Bronze cracks. The bell splits from crown to lip, and its voice ends in a harsh, broken clang. Matěj collapses. Without the bell’s borrowed power, the wound in his throat opens again. Alucard rises before the priest has finished dying. He steps over Matěj and stops in front of Yennefer. His coat is whole; the stone beneath it is still wet with his blood. “You could have bound me while I was dead,” he says. “For how long?” His smile returns. “Now that is an honest answer.” Beyond the chapel, the wolves call across the forest at uneven intervals. One voice sounds close to the abbey wall; another answers from miles away. Yennefer leads the child toward the doors. Alucard follows, keeping just far enough back that she cannot mistake it for obedience.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric writing, successfully creating a dark medieval encounter between two powerful supernatural beings. The author effectively captures the essence of both characters - Alucard's sadistic confidence and death-seeking nature, and Yennefer's pragmatic ambition and hidden vulnerabilities. The story structure is well-constructed, opening with atmospheric tension and building to a supernatural confrontation involving a corrupted priest and a magical bell. The pacing moves efficiently from initial encounter to collaborative action, maintaining tension throughout. The dialogue is particularly strong, with exchanges that feel authentic to both characters while advancing plot and revealing personality. Character portrayal shows nuanced understanding of the source material. Alucard's willingness to die for a worthy challenge feels completely in character, as does his predatory interest in Yennefer's power. Yennefer's internal conflict between self-interest and protecting innocents captures her complex morality well. The power dynamic shifts naturally as promised in the prompt. The prose style is atmospheric without becoming overwrought, using concrete imagery effectively - the red moonlight, the chapel setting, the bronze bell's supernatural resonance. Sentences flow naturally and the third-person present tense is handled skillfully. However, the story suffers from some predictable elements. The corrupted priest antagonist and magical artifact plot feel somewhat formulaic for the fantasy genre. The resolution, while satisfying, doesn't surprise. The ending maintains appropriate darkness without false positivity, though it leaves the central tension between the protagonists unresolved in a way that feels incomplete rather than intriguingly open. The emotional complexity is present but could be deeper - Yennefer's temptation by the bell's promise feels underdeveloped, and Alucard's psychology, while accurate to character, remains somewhat surface-level. The piece engages the reader effectively but doesn't reach the heights of truly memorable fiction. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. Model Output:
The first camera dies at 9:17. Jolyne knows because she is watching its red light when Makima passes beneath it. The light blinks once and goes dark. Farther down the corridor, a second camera follows. “Old wiring,” says the guard escorting them. Makima smiles at him. “That must be it.” The guard looks relieved to have agreed with her. Jolyne’s wrists are cuffed, but a thread of Stone Free runs from her fingertip along the seam of her sleeve. It brushes the wall as they walk, carrying voices back to her through the concrete. Behind the observation-room door, somebody is crying. “Where are you taking me?” Jolyne asks. “To meet a friend of yours,” Makima says. Her voice is soft enough to make the cuffs feel like a misunderstanding. “Tessa Moreno.” Jolyne stops. Tessa is in the infirmary, or she was an hour ago. She has a fever and a habit of calling every supernatural thing in the prison *ghost shit*, including the thing that took her left hand. Makima stops too. “You’ve been trying to get her transferred.” “Yeah. Away from here.” “That’s possible.” Jolyne looks at her. Auburn hair, tidy coat, eyes like yellow targets nested inside one another. Makima holds her gaze with patient interest. “What do you want?” Jolyne asks. “To see how your ability works.” A guard opens the observation-room door. Tessa sits at a table inside, her remaining hand flat on a sheet of paper. A pen lies beside it. There are two chairs across from her. “No,” Jolyne says. “It’s only a consent form,” Makima replies. “Tessa can leave tonight if she signs.” Tessa looks up. “She said you’d come.” Jolyne sends her thread beneath the table. It touches the leg of Tessa’s chair, then the corner of the paper. The top line names a transfer facility. Below it, in smaller print, Tessa agrees to participate in further study until the transfer is approved. Makima watches Jolyne’s cuffed hand. “Can you read through the string?” Jolyne yanks the thread back. “Can you tell the truth through your teeth?” Makima’s smile holds. The guard takes a step toward Jolyne, but Makima raises one finger and he stays where he is. “Tessa,” Makima says, “you want to leave, don’t you?” Tessa picks up the pen. Stone Free snaps out of Jolyne’s shoulder. Blue strings hook the pen and rip it from Tessa’s hand. The guard lunges. Jolyne loops his ankles and drops him hard enough to make his keys skid across the floor. The third camera goes dark. For a moment, nobody moves. Jolyne feels her strings stretched between the guard and the table; she can pull Tessa away from the door, or hold the guard down, but not both without unraveling more of herself. Makima looks at the strings. “Does it hurt?” “When it gets torn.” Makima nods, as though Jolyne has answered a reasonable question. Then she turns to Tessa. “You could ask her to stop,” Makima says. “She came because you were frightened. She’ll listen to you.” Tessa’s eyes fill. “Jolyne, please. I just want out.” Jolyne almost lets the guard go. Instead she tightens the string around his legs and turns to Tessa. “Read the bottom part,” she says. Tessa pulls the paper closer. Her lips move. She reaches the final paragraph and goes still. Makima says, “It’s a temporary arrangement.” “How long?” Tessa asks. “That depends on what we learn.” Jolyne sees Tessa set the paper down. Then Makima says her name. “Tessa.” The girl sits straight. The guard, still tangled on the floor, falls quiet too. Jolyne hears footsteps through the corridor wall—more guards coming toward the room. Makima has not raised her voice. She takes the chair opposite Tessa and folds her hands on the table. “You’re afraid your friend will be hurt,” she tells her. “I understand.” Tessa’s hand moves back toward the paper. Jolyne pulls a string from beneath her fingernail and sends it into the door’s lock. Metal scrapes. Makima glances over, fascinated despite herself. That is all Jolyne needs. She has another strand inside the table, running beneath the sheet to its far edge. Stone Free yanks the paper apart. One piece stays under Tessa’s hand; the other whips into the air. Jolyne catches it, crushes it, and stuffs it into her mouth. The footsteps break into a run. The lock gives way under her string. “Go!” Jolyne shouts. Tessa bolts through the door. The first guard coming around the corner catches a fistful of Stone Free to the face. Jolyne shoves Tessa past him toward the stairwell. Makima remains seated. “She won’t make it through the outer gate.” “Then open it,” Jolyne says. Makima studies her. “You destroyed the form.” “You’ve got a printer.” “Why would I open the gate?” Jolyne points at the dead camera above her. The one at the corridor junction is dark as well; she can see it past the fallen guard. “They say the cameras always do that when you walk by. I figured somebody was watching the recordings anyway.” For the first time, Makima’s expression changes. It is slight: a pause before she speaks. Jolyne pulls her last loose thread. In the corridor, the guard’s radio clicks on. She has wound the strand through its switch and into the speaker grille. The open channel carries Makima’s voice from the room, and Tessa’s, and the guard’s groan as he tries to stand. “Control room,” Jolyne calls into it. “You hear us? Pull Tessa Moreno’s file. Look for the transfer form.” Makima rises. Jolyne braces for a command, for something worse than the guards. Instead, Makima says, “You’re very resourceful.” The radio crackles. “We hear you,” a woman says. “Open the outer gate for Moreno,” Jolyne tells her. A long silence follows. Makima looks toward the speaker. Whatever she might say to the woman in the control room, she cannot do it privately. At last the radio answers. “Gate opening.” Jolyne hears the mechanism through the strings in the wall. It is distant, but unmistakable. Tessa’s shoes pound down the stairs. Makima steps close enough to touch Jolyne’s butterfly tattoo. Jolyne coils Stone Free around her own arm and holds still. “The cameras aren’t all broken,” Makima says. “Good.” For several seconds they listen to Tessa run. Then a buzzer sounds beyond the stairwell, followed by the heavy slam of the outer gate. Makima withdraws her hand. “We’ll speak again.” Jolyne looks at the radio in the guard’s hand. Its channel is still open, and the woman in the control room is still listening. “Yeah,” she says. “Maybe with a witness next time.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This story demonstrates strong technical execution and character understanding within the supernatural prison setting. The author effectively captures both characters' essential traits - Jolyne's protective instincts and resourceful use of Stone Free, and Makima's manipulative nature masked by false pleasantness. The premise of using Tessa as leverage creates immediate tension and stakes. The prose is clean and purposeful, with particularly effective use of concrete details like the dying cameras and Jolyne's string threading through various objects. The author shows strong command of "show don't tell," revealing character motivations and abilities through action rather than exposition. Makima's control powers are demonstrated subtly through the guard's behavior and Tessa's responses, while Jolyne's Stand ability is woven naturally into the action. The dialogue feels authentic to both characters, with Jolyne's directness contrasting sharply with Makima's deceptively gentle manipulation. The escalating tension builds effectively as Jolyne realizes the trap and uses her abilities creatively to both gather information and create leverage. However, the story suffers from some pacing issues in the middle section, and the resolution, while clever, feels somewhat mechanical. The use of the radio as a surveillance tool is creative but the final confrontation lacks the psychological depth that could have elevated the piece. The ending is competent but doesn't fully capitalize on the rich character dynamics established earlier. The writing maintains consistent tone throughout and avoids common pitfalls like purple prose or overwrought emotion. The supernatural elements are integrated naturally without excessive explanation. While solid overall, the piece doesn't quite reach the level of exceptional creativity or emotional resonance that would make it truly memorable. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-7841 **Document Type:** Researcher’s Report, First-Person Account **Author:** Dr. Mara Venn **Status:** Written under observation I found the first note beneath my coffee cup at 08:12 on a Tuesday. It was folded once, written on yellow legal paper, and addressed to me in my handwriting. > **Mara—** > > **At 14:07, there will be a breach in Wing C. Do not authorize the transfer.** > > **You will think you have time to check this. You do not.** I was responsible for the transfer of SCP-4419, a contained entity associated with false autobiographical memories. Its chamber required maintenance, and the scheduled move was at 14:00. I canceled it. At 14:07, nothing happened. Wing C remained secure. I filed the note as a possible manifestation of SCP-4419 and submitted myself for evaluation. Security reviewed my office footage. At 08:12:03, every camera covering my desk lost one frame. Before it, the paper was absent. After it, the paper was under my cup. The cameras used separate power supplies and recording systems. None showed me touching the cup. The next note appeared two mornings later, in the middle of a clean desk. Again, the cameras glitched at the exact moment it appeared. > **Canceling the transfer only changed the hour. They will call this manipulation. You called it manipulation the first time, too.** > > **Ask Havel what happened to his left hand.** Dr. Havel had both hands. He permitted a scan, partly because he wanted the matter resolved and partly, I suspected, because he thought I needed reassurance. The scan found no injury. When I told him about the note, he said SCP-4419 had probably learned his name from my interviews. That was reasonable. SCP-4419’s recorded effects included convincing staff that they had attended meetings that had never occurred. It had once persuaded a guard that he remembered raising a daughter. The guard had no children. We placed my desk under continuous observation. I wore a camera. A technician sealed the office vents and inventoried every sheet of paper in the room. The third note appeared while six people watched through the glass. I was seated with my hands in my lap. The room’s four cameras glitched simultaneously. My body camera did not record a glitch, but its next frame showed the note where the previous frame had shown bare wood. None of us saw it arrive. We all saw it afterward. > **His hand was taken in the breach. This is earlier than the hand.** > > **The chamber has a second door. Please believe me before you see it.** There was no second door. Engineering removed the chamber’s wall panels and found uninterrupted concrete. I watched them do it, then returned at night to make certain they had replaced the panels. I could no longer remember whether I had seen four workers or five. The Foundation tested both hypotheses. Temporal Studies compared the notes’ ink with our supply. It matched a pen issued to me, although chemical analysis indicated the ink had dried months before that batch was manufactured. Psychologists interviewed me apart from SCP-4419 personnel and found no evidence that I had been prompted to write the notes. A handwriting specialist identified the writing as mine, with changes consistent with severe fatigue and an injury to my right wrist. My wrist was uninjured. I began checking it when I woke. The fourth note predicted that an alarm would sound at 14:07. We isolated Wing C, disabled its alarm network, and stationed technicians beside the disconnected sirens. At 14:07, every technician reported hearing an alarm. Their audio equipment recorded silence. I heard it from my office. It lasted eleven seconds. Afterward, Dr. Havel asked whether I had known about the alarm in advance. I showed him the note again. He read it twice and told me the page was blank. It was not blank to me. We photographed it; the photograph showed writing. Havel apologized, then asked to see it a third time. He saw the writing that time. He requested removal from the investigation. I requested removal as well. The request was denied because I had become the only reliable subject of the notes, and because “reliable” had acquired a narrow meaning. I tried to establish facts I could carry from one day to the next. I wrote my name on my forearm. I recorded my mother’s voice so that I would recognize it. I counted the doors between my office and SCP-4419’s chamber. The fifth note was on my desk when I finished counting. > **Mother died when you were nine. The voice is hers, but she has been dead for thirty years.** > > **Do not count the doors again. It notices when you do.** My mother answered the telephone that evening. She was angry that I had called only to ask what year it was. I was relieved until she mentioned a dog we had owned when I was seven. I remembered burying him behind our house. She said he had run away. Neither memory had anything to do with containment. That made the disagreement harder to dismiss. I stopped calling her. I also stopped calling events “changes.” I had no evidence that anything had changed, only evidence that I could not trust my account of what had been there before. SCP-4419 was capable of exploiting precisely that distinction. Temporal Studies argued that it could not have altered the ink or interrupted the cameras. Psychology argued that we did not know what SCP-4419 could do. The sixth note appeared during a site-wide power test. At the instant it appeared, the battery-backed cameras covering my desk glitched. No other camera in the facility did. > **I let it out.** > > **I thought the second door led into the chamber. I thought I was bringing someone home.** > > **Mara, when Havel has no hand, it will be too late to ask him to stop you.** I asked Security to confine me. They agreed. They searched my office and took away my keys, my pen, and my access badge. I wrote this report in an observation room while a guard watched from the corridor. I did not tell him about the last note until I had copied it here. It appeared on the table at 08:12. The room’s camera glitched. The guard swore and came inside. He saw the paper before I touched it. > **This was the report you wrote before the breach.** > > **I am sorry I kept calling them warnings.** The guard took the note. I asked him to check his hands. He held them up for me, both intact, and said we were still safe. I believed him while he was speaking.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP report demonstrates strong adherence to the Foundation's clinical documentation style while effectively employing first-person narration to create mounting psychological tension. The author successfully captures the bureaucratic tone characteristic of SCP entries while maintaining the researcher's increasingly fragmented mental state. The piece excels in its structural approach, using the format of timestamped notes and clinical observations to build dread. The temporal anomaly concept is well-executed, with each note escalating both the supernatural threat and the protagonist's psychological deterioration. The contradiction between objective reality and subjective experience creates genuine uncertainty about whether Dr. Venn is experiencing a temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation. Character development is subtle but effective. Dr. Venn's transformation from confident researcher to paranoid, isolated individual feels organic. Her attempts to establish objective facts (writing on her arm, recording her mother's voice, counting doors) demonstrate believable responses to reality breakdown. The supporting characters, particularly Dr. Havel, serve their functions well within the constrained format. The prose maintains clinical precision while building atmospheric dread. Details like the camera glitches, the ink analysis showing impossible aging, and the gradual revelation of memory inconsistencies create a compelling sense of unreality. The author avoids purple prose while still generating strong imagery through precise, unsettling details. However, the piece has some weaknesses. The ending, while thematically appropriate, feels somewhat abrupt and could benefit from stronger resolution. Some plot elements, like the mother's contradictory memories about the dog, feel slightly disconnected from the main narrative thread. The dialogue, while functional, lacks distinctive character voices and serves primarily plot advancement rather than character development. The emotional complexity is strong, particularly in conveying Dr. Venn's growing isolation and self-doubt. The piece successfully generates paranoia and uncertainty in the reader, making them question the reliability of the narrator alongside the Foundation personnel. + Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 79.3
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-7841 **Object Class:** Euclid **Special Containment Procedures:** Confirmed SCP-7841 entrances are to be concealed within their host buildings. Demolition orders affecting those buildings require approval from the SCP-7841 research team. Reports of unmarked doors in abandoned structures, particularly doors emitting light after local power has been disconnected, are to be investigated. Personnel entering SCP-7841 must remain within sight of an entrance. Documents may be photographed but not removed without written authorization. No team is to pursue the personnel described in Exploration Log 7841-6. **Description:** SCP-7841 is an archive accessible through identical doors that have appeared in abandoned buildings on six continents. Each door is unmarked, painted a dull cream color, and fitted with a brass handle. Its frame is not joined to the surrounding wall by any detectable means. In complete darkness, a faint white glow escapes through its edges. All confirmed doors open into the same apparent structure: a sequence of reading rooms, storage halls, stairwells, and cataloging stations of indeterminate extent. Rooms observed from a distance have sometimes been found behind the exploration team after a turn. One stairwell has been measured descending 412 meters below a building with no basement; a window beside its lowest landing looked onto the roof of that building. The archive contains documents in numerous languages, including languages not otherwise attested. Much of its material describes a previous global civilization, designated **Civilization A**, whose institutions, communications systems, and population distribution were broadly comparable to those of the present day. Surviving records give no consistent date for its destruction. They refer instead to a single “containment failure,” without identifying what was contained. The first entrance was discovered in 2023, inside a disused municipal hospital in São Paulo. Entrances have since been found in former offices, schools, factories, and places of worship. No door has appeared in an occupied building. **Recovered Document 7841-12:** *Summary for District Custodians*, retrieved from Reading Room 4. > The failure was not local. District custodians are instructed to discontinue use of maps showing an unaffected region. > > Requests for the name of the contained item are to be returned unanswered. The name was removed from the incident record under Closure Order 1. This does not indicate that the item was destroyed. > > Persons reaching a repository entrance should be admitted. Recording their names remains necessary even when those names are already present. The Foundation first appeared in SCP-7841 records under the name **Office of Continuity**. Early researchers considered it an unrelated organization with similar containment duties. That assessment was withdrawn after personnel records were found for current Foundation staff. **Recovered Document 7841-31:** *Office of Continuity Personnel Register*, folio dated 18 September 1694. > **Employee:** Dr. Mara Velez > **Assignment:** Catalog integrity, western repository > **Status:** Active > **Access restriction:** Employee is not to be informed that the second register has been opened. Prior notification resulted in refusal to continue work. The folio includes Dr. Velez’s fingerprints, dental chart, and a photograph identical in appearance to her current Foundation identification image. Dr. Velez was born in 1981. She has no recollection of the Office of Continuity or of visiting SCP-7841 before its discovery. Forty-three further matches have been verified. Their files are dated between 1622 and 1710. In nine cases, the recorded assignment describes an event that the employee would later encounter while working for the Foundation. **Exploration Log 7841-6:** Entrance through an abandoned railway office, Poland. Team consisted of Captain Okafor, Dr. Velez, and two security personnel. Body-camera times are retained below. **09:14:** The team entered a catalog hall whose shelves extended above the range of its lights. Several empty spaces interrupted otherwise complete runs of numbered volumes. Paper scraps lay beneath them. **09:19:** Dr. Velez found a wheeled cart loaded with tied document bundles. Each bundle bore a floor and aisle designation. A fresh pencil mark had been drawn through every designation on the nearby wall directory. **09:23:** The team heard metal striking metal beyond a partition. Captain Okafor moved to the end of the aisle and observed four figures wearing hooded protective suits. Their faceplates were opaque. Two figures were carrying a shelving unit through a doorway too narrow to accommodate it. When Captain Okafor announced the team’s presence, all four figures stopped. One turned its faceplate toward Dr. Velez. The figures then abandoned the shelving unit and ran. The team did not pursue them. **09:25:** The partition behind the figures was found to be a solid wall. The shelving unit and the documents on the cart were gone. In their place, the wall directory listed an aisle the team had not seen on entry. **09:31:** The team reached that aisle. It held 43 empty personnel folders. One folder was labeled with Dr. Velez’s current Foundation employee number, issued in 2016. Following Log 7841-6, entrances were placed under continuous camera surveillance. No suited figures have been recorded entering from outside. They have since been observed on three expeditions, each time removing shelves, documents, or catalog fixtures. They retreat when Foundation personnel approach. None has attempted to interfere with an exploration team. During a review of catalog requests, researchers found a visitor ledger at a desk close to the São Paulo entrance. Its most recent page contained five signatures matching those of serving O5 Council members. Beside each signature was a date within the preceding month and an impression from a Foundation access seal. Examination of the seal impressions confirmed that they had been made by the Council’s current authentication devices. No visit to SCP-7841 appears in the Foundation’s entry logs. The Council stated that it had authorized no such visits. After copies of the ledger were submitted for review, its original page was removed from the archive. The desk remained; the binding threads where the page had been attached were newly cut. A carbon sheet beneath the ledger preserved part of a note written on the missing page: > The Council has inspected the cleared sections. Removal remains behind schedule. The returning staff must not be allowed to compare the registers. Dr. Velez requested that her archive access be suspended. The request was granted. Three days later, surveillance at the sealed hospital entrance in São Paulo recorded its door opening inward. No person appeared in the corridor. When the door closed, a personnel folder lay outside it. The folder contained Dr. Velez’s current access card and an appointment notice bearing the Office of Continuity seal. The notice was dated the following morning.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP entry demonstrates strong technical execution and adherence to the Foundation's clinical documentation style. The author successfully captures the bureaucratic tone characteristic of SCP entries while weaving together multiple complex narrative threads involving temporal anomalies, organizational mysteries, and existential implications. The piece excels in its structural coherence, presenting information in a logical progression from basic containment procedures through increasingly disturbing revelations. The concept of doors leading to an impossible archive containing records of a previous civilization is compelling, and the connection to the Foundation's own history through the "Office of Continuity" creates effective narrative tension. The writing maintains consistent voice throughout, never breaking from the clinical, matter-of-fact tone that makes SCP entries effective. The author skillfully uses this restraint to make the more unsettling elements—like Dr. Velez's centuries-old personnel file with her current photograph—more impactful through understatement rather than melodrama. The exploration logs and recovered documents feel authentic to the format while advancing the plot effectively. The mysterious hazmat-suited figures removing materials adds kinetic tension to what could have been a static archive setting. The revelation about unauthorized O5 Council visits and the final scene with Dr. Velez's appointment notice creates a satisfying escalation of stakes. However, the piece has some limitations in character development. While Dr. Velez serves as an effective focal point for the temporal mystery, she remains largely a plot device rather than a fully realized character. The other personnel are even more thinly sketched. The dialogue, while minimal and appropriate to the format, doesn't reveal much about individual personalities. The imagery is functional but not particularly evocative. Descriptions serve the plot well but rarely create memorable visual moments. The "dull cream color" doors and "faint white glow" are adequate but unremarkable details. The ending strikes an appropriate note of unresolved tension without being artificially dark or light. The appointment notice dated for the following morning creates genuine unease about Dr. Velez's fate while maintaining the Foundation's characteristic inability to fully control anomalous phenomena. + Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 83.2
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The first thing the colony taught Tavi was that its maps were honest only about streets. On the command map, Pel’s Cross was a square bordered by the Hall of Accord, the transit station, and four approved lodging houses. At ground level it was a basin of steps and awnings. Water ran down its center in a stone channel. Children hopped across it, going nowhere that Tavi could see. The reception in the Hall was meant to last until dusk. Tavi had been introduced as the youngest envoy ever appointed to the mission, a distinction Command seemed to consider both useful and regrettable. During a speech about “the colony’s three settled peoples,” Tavi left by a service door. The market below the square smelled of hot oil, rain on stone, and something sharp and mineral. Stalls sold handwoven fabrics dyed in pigments not found on Earth: a blue that held a green glint when folded, a dark orange that seemed to gather light in its creases. An old man at one stall laid a length of cloth across Tavi’s wrists. “For the hall?” he asked. “No.” “Then you can afford to like it.” His hands were broad, with the extra joint Tavi had seen in Command’s anatomical briefings. The briefings called his lineage the Reach. They had developed in the lowland marshes after the first settlements lost contact. Another lineage, the Stone, had been isolated in the uplands for eleven generations. The third, the Hearth, were described as closest to the landing population, though the briefings supplied no measure of closeness. A small woman ducked beneath the hanging cloth and gave the old man a spool of thread. Her pupils were narrow in the daylight. She wore a child on her back, asleep under a hood. Stone, according to the briefing. The child’s long fingers curled around her collar. “Your daughter?” Tavi asked. “My niece,” said the woman. “His granddaughter.” The old man looked up. “Is that a problem where you come from?” “No.” “Good. It’s been enough of one here.” She went on through the market. Tavi paid for the cloth and followed at a distance, not to learn anything in particular now, but because she had used a stair Tavi hadn’t noticed. The stair opened onto a courtyard roofed with clear tiles. People sat at tables beneath them, repairing pumps, sorting seed, arguing over a slate of numbers. At the far end, two clerks occupied a booth marked **Petitions: Water, Work, Kinship**. A man with the dark, reflective skin common among the Reach was explaining a drainage failure to one clerk while a pale Hearth woman corrected his measurements. Neither deferred to the other. When the clerk asked who had standing to submit the petition, both raised their hands. Tavi had been instructed to ask the governor whether the lineages could be persuaded to share responsibility for the canals. A bell rang. The people at the tables took up their tools and began to leave. The pale woman remained to add a final figure to the petition. Tavi stayed long enough to see the clerk stamp it, then returned to the Hall. Command was waiting in Tavi’s quarters. “You went out without escort,” Commander Vale said. She stood beside the window, still wearing her reception collar. “We had three people looking for you.” “I’m sorry they had to.” “That is not what I need from you.” Tavi set the folded cloth on the desk. Vale glanced at it, then at Tavi’s shoes, which were dusty from the market steps. “You were sent to address a dispute,” she said. “If one faction had chosen to make you part of it, an apology would be of little use.” “I understand.” “I don’t think you do yet.” Vale’s voice softened, which made the rebuke worse. “Tomorrow the governor will tell us the uplands are withholding labor. The upland delegation will tell us the lowlands control the water. We need to know who can act, not simply who can speak.” “There’s a petitions court below Pel’s Cross. I watched a Reach man and a Hearth woman file together over a canal.” Vale was silent for a moment. “The court has no recognized authority in the colonial charter.” “They appeared to expect an answer.” “They may get one. That doesn’t mean the governor will honor it.” Vale moved toward the door. “Minister Sen asked to meet you tonight. I had intended to postpone it. Go now, and let him do the asking.” The Minister of Science received Tavi in a room lined with field instruments. A wind gauge stood beside a cabinet of soil cores. Sen sat at a table reading a report and did not rise. “You visited the market,” he said. “Yes.” “Vale will be annoyed with me if I seem to approve.” “Do you?” “I haven’t decided.” He turned a page. “What did you find?” “Cloth. A courtyard where people petition about the canals.” He looked up. “I appointed the clerks.” Tavi considered this. “Does the governor know?” “Of course. She approves their wages. She cannot publicly approve their judgments.” He set the report down. “The colonial charter assigns water rights to the founding households. Some no longer exist. Others have descendants in every lineage. The court gives people somewhere to bring a broken pump without first proving which ancestor owned it.” “And the petitions?” “Come to me. When I can settle them, I do. When I can’t, they remain on my desk.” He tapped the report. “What did you think my ministry studied?” “Adaptation. Inheritance.” “That is what the instruments are for. My predecessor used some of them.” Sen poured water into two cups. He pushed one toward Tavi, then waited until Tavi drank. His expression did not change. “The governor wants an offworld commission,” he said. “The upland delegates want you to reject one. Commander Vale wants a route through the dispute that will hold after your ship leaves. What do you want?” Tavi put down the cup. “To know why the governor won’t recognize a court she pays for.” “She would have to amend the charter. The founding households would lose claims they still value.” “Can she amend it?” “With the Assembly.” “And will the Assembly sit?” Sen’s mouth tightened. “Not if the governor can persuade your commission to make the decision for them.” At last Tavi understood why he had asked for this meeting. An offworld ruling would let every local office object to the result while obeying it. “You could have told Command about the court,” Tavi said. “I have. Your predecessors met the governor and read the charter. They thought a court without a place in it was temporary.” “Perhaps it is.” “It has been open for twenty-six years.” Tavi looked at the instruments, carefully dusted by someone who knew they might be used again. “If Command proposes a commission, will you support it?” “I asked first.” “Then I can’t answer for Command.” Tavi stood. “I’ll tell Vale what you told me, and ask her to visit the court before we meet the governor.” Sen’s gaze went to the cloth beneath Tavi’s arm. “You might tell her to go by the market steps. The other entrance has been closed for repairs.” Outside, the light had gone from the square. Tavi could not see the water channel from Sen’s window, but could hear it, running steadily under the voices below.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of Ursula K. Le Guin's literary style, particularly her approach to anthropological science fiction and political complexity. The writing successfully captures Le Guin's characteristic restraint, her focus on social structures over action, and her ability to reveal deeper truths through seemingly mundane interactions. The worldbuilding is expertly handled through subtle details rather than exposition dumps. The three human subspecies (Reach, Stone, Hearth) are introduced naturally through physical observations and social interactions. The author shows considerable skill in revealing the political complexity through layers - the official briefings versus ground reality, the unofficial court system, and the web of competing interests between governor, minister, and offworld command. The protagonist Tavi is well-characterized through actions and choices rather than internal monologue. The decision to slip away from official functions feels authentic for a young diplomat, and the character's growing understanding of the political situation unfolds naturally. The supporting characters, particularly Minister Sen, are nuanced and avoid simple categorization. The dialogue is particularly strong, especially in the conversation with Sen. It feels natural while carrying significant political weight. Sen's testing of Tavi through seemingly casual conversation demonstrates sophisticated character work. The exchanges reveal information organically while maintaining tension. The prose style successfully emulates Le Guin's elegant simplicity. Sentences are clean and purposeful without being sparse. The imagery is vivid but not overwrought - the description of the dyed fabrics, the water channel, and the courtyard with clear tiles creates a lived-in world without excessive detail. The political intrigue is genuinely complex and avoids easy resolutions. The unofficial court system that operates with tacit approval but no official recognition is exactly the kind of anthropological detail Le Guin would explore. The ending leaves appropriate questions unresolved while providing Tavi with new understanding. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the political exposition becomes slightly heavy-handed, and a few instances where character motivations could be more clearly established. The pacing is generally strong but slows slightly during the middle market sequence. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 79.8
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Polymerase Chain Reaction Glow-in-the-dark mushrooms sprouted in the cracked lab tiles, remnants of old splicing tests. Mara had stopped trying to pull them out. They returned within days, lighting the floor in pale green commas that showed her where to step when the generator failed. Tonight the generator was failing often. The centrifuge had once belonged to a dental clinic. Its lid was held down by a bicycle lock, and somebody had painted *DO NOT OPEN* over the faded picture of a smiling tooth. The thermal cycler was a bread maker fitted with parts from three dead hospital machines. Every time it changed temperature, the kettle beside it clicked in sympathy. On Mara’s bench sat six grains of barley. “Six?” said Niko. “Six that grew from their own seed.” Mara kept her eyes on the bench. “The rest grew fine and left us nothing.” Before the collapse, Veyne Agricultural had sold the settlement’s grandparents a harvest that could feed a town. The plants grew fast in poor soil. Their grain made strong flour. The seed saved from that harvest looked sound too, right up until planting, when the engineered sections of its DNA came apart. Veyne called it a licensing safeguard. Growers who wanted another harvest bought another packet. Then the trucks stopped coming. Mara had spent the winter pulling usable fragments from frozen seed catalogs and splicing them into the hardy, bitter barley that grew wild along the railway. Most of her test plants died. Some grew leaves but no grain. Six had lived long enough for her to plant their seed and see a second crop come up. Niko leaned against the doorframe. “The buyer’s here.” Mara slipped the grains into a folded square of paper. “Did you tell her six?” “I told her you had what the contract asked for.” “That isn’t what I asked you.” “And the pump filters she brought aren’t what the south field can do without.” He was right. Silt had worn through the last filter mesh. The irrigation pump spat mud into the furrows now. They had perhaps two weeks before it seized, and less if the rain held off. Mara picked up the paper packet and followed him upstairs. The buyer waited in the old school cafeteria beneath a ceiling stained by last year’s floods. She wore clean boots and a gray coat with every label cut out. Two sealed filter cylinders sat on the table in front of her. “Dr. Voss,” she said. “Mara.” “I’m Sera. May I see the proof?” Mara laid the packet on the table but kept two fingers on it. Sera unfolded a contract screen between them. Its glass was scratched; the text was sharp. Payment: two pump filters, delivery tonight. Mara’s end: six viable second-generation seeds, their parent plants, and all records of the work. Exclusive ownership of the resulting line. No distribution without buyer approval. “You want the crop from our test plot,” Mara said. “I want what I’m paying for.” “You’re paying for filters. You’re asking for our next harvest.” Sera glanced at Niko. “He said you understood the terms.” Niko’s jaw tightened. Mara didn’t look at him. She scrolled farther. At the bottom was a clause requiring the grower to maintain “approved generational limits.” Mara read it twice. “You want me to put the failure back.” Sera reached for the packet. Mara lifted it away. “Not failure,” Sera said. “Control. A reliable grain supply needs a reliable supplier.” “We tried that.” Outside, a cart rattled over the broken paving. Mara could hear children calling to one another at the water tank. The school’s windows were covered with boards, but a thin line of evening light fell across the contract. Sera noticed Mara watching it. “Those filters took me nine days to find. You can keep your harvest this year. Next year you’ll need parts again. I can get them.” Mara’s left hand began to ache. She pressed it flat on the table until the shaking eased. Three winters ago, an untested treatment had cleared an infection from her lungs when the clinic had run out of antibiotics. It had also left bands of dense tissue along her ribs and forearm. Cold made them hurt. Breathing deeply hurt. But she could spend an hour in the mold-heavy basement lab without the fever that laid other workers low, and her thickened fingertips barely felt the hot casing of the temperamental bread maker. She had kept working because the treatment let her. On bad mornings, she wondered how much longer it would. “The clause is standard,” Sera said. Mara laughed once. “So were Veyne’s seed packets.” Sera’s face changed. Only a little, but enough. “You worked for them,” Mara said. “My mother did. I read her files after she died.” Sera folded her hands. “I know what you’ve made. Anyone who can make it can make more. If I take these to the market, someone will copy them and sell them cheaper within a season. Then I can’t buy another filter, and neither can you.” “People could grow food.” “For a season. After that, who keeps the pumps running?” Mara thought of the six short rows in the schoolyard test plot, and of the grain drying in sacks beneath Niko’s bed. Enough to plant part of the south field if the pump held. Not enough to gamble away. She pushed the packet into her pocket. “New terms. The filters stay. You take two grains and my growth records. By tomorrow, every settlement on this canal gets a copy of the records and seed from our next harvest.” Sera shook her head. “That’s not a sale.” “No.” Mara turned the screen and began deleting. “You can charge for finding parts. You can charge to carry grain. You can’t own what grows from it.” Niko stared at her. “Mara, if she leaves—” “The filters are on the table,” Sera said. “I haven’t left.” For a while she watched Mara edit. Then she took the screen and read the new terms all the way through. She changed *next harvest* to *first viable surplus*. Mara changed it back and added a minimum weight. They argued over transport and settled on the canal, where Sera already ran a boat. At last Sera pressed her thumb to the glass. Mara signed beneath it. Niko carried the filters away before either woman could reconsider. Sera held out her hand for the two grains. Mara counted them into her palm. They looked too small to bear the price of anything. “How do I know they’ll grow?” Sera asked. “You don’t,” Mara said. “Plant them.” Downstairs, the generator caught, faltered, and caught again. Through the open stairwell came the warm smell of dust from the bread maker. Mara still had four grains to test, a field waiting for water, and no guarantee that the next generation would survive. She went back to work while the lights were on.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This biopunk story successfully creates a compelling post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering has left communities struggling with deliberately obsolescent crops. The author demonstrates strong world-building through specific, tactile details like the glow-in-the-dark mushrooms, jury-rigged equipment (dental clinic centrifuge, bread maker thermal cycler), and the physical modifications Mara bears from untested treatments. The central conflict around the black market contract is well-constructed, with clear stakes and moral complexity. Mara's dilemma between immediate survival needs (the pump filters) and long-term community welfare creates genuine tension. The negotiation scene effectively shows character through action and dialogue, particularly in how Mara rewrites the contract terms to prevent another cycle of corporate control. Character development is nuanced, especially Mara's portrayal as someone bearing both the costs and benefits of experimental medicine. Her physical pain from past treatments contrasts with her enhanced ability to work in harsh conditions, creating a believable character shaped by her environment. Sera's revelation as the daughter of a former Veyne employee adds depth to the antagonist role. The prose is generally clean and evocative without being overwrought. Descriptions like "pale green commas" for the mushrooms and the "warm smell of dust from the bread maker" create atmosphere without excess. The technical details feel researched and authentic to the biopunk genre. However, some elements could be stronger. The dialogue, while functional, occasionally feels slightly stilted in places. The ending, while thematically appropriate, resolves perhaps too neatly given the complexity of the situation. The story also relies somewhat heavily on exposition in places, though this is largely necessary for world-building. The piece successfully fulfills the prompt requirements, incorporating all requested elements: the post-apocalyptic setting, obsolescent genetic engineering, jury-rigged equipment, physical modifications, and the black market contract plot. The 1000-word length is well-utilized.
