+ Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 82.8
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Polymerase Chain Reaction The contract arrived in a jar of honey. Mara held it to the lamp. Beneath the amber syrup floated a strip of black plastic, rolled tight enough to fit through the jar’s neck. On it, in white type, were three lines: **TWELVE VIABLE BRASSICA LINES.** **DELIVERY BEFORE FIRST FROST.** **PAYMENT: ONE UNLICENSED MATERNAL SEED LOT.** She read the last line twice. Outside the greenhouse, Settlement Nine’s children were stripping yellow leaves from the final stand of winter cabbage. Their parents had saved seed from last year’s crop, as their parents had done before the corporate farms. Half of it had failed to sprout. The rest had grown leaves too thin to survive a cold snap. One harvest. That was what the companies had sold, right up to the collapse. Corn that fed a town brilliantly and left sterile kernels. Rice that grew in salt water until its offspring lost the trait. The contracts called it *licensed continuity*. Mara called it hunger with paperwork. She opened the jar. The honey smelled real. Her lab occupied the shell of an old bus. Bicycle chains drove a salvaged centrifuge. A refrigerator compressor cooled the storage box; when the electricity failed, wet cloth and night air did what they could. The thermal cycler had once belonged to a veterinary clinic. Its display was dead, so Mara judged its moods by the clicking relay and the cheap thermometer wired through the lid. Across the workbench stood six empty canisters from Helixor, the biotech giant that had patented most of the region’s food. Their labels still promised *a better tomorrow, every season*. Mara had scrubbed them clean and filled them with the few reagents she had left. Every time she reached for one, Helixor’s bright green logo flashed under her hand. She unrolled the plastic strip. The broker’s mark was punched into one corner: a tiny square hole inside a larger one. Pell. He had bought medicines for Settlement Nine before, and sold them at a profit to someone else. A second strip lay inside the first. **CLIENT PROVIDES SOURCE MATERIAL. NO QUESTIONS.** By dusk, a stranger brought a packet of seeds wrapped in three layers of oilcloth. She wore a patched raincoat and carried a pistol with no magazine. “Where did Pell get these?” Mara asked. “He didn’t,” the stranger said. “I did.” Mara tipped a few seeds into her palm. Brassica, by their shape. Dark, sound, and impossibly old if the handwriting on the packet was genuine. **MOTHER STOCK. DO NOT DISTRIBUTE.** The stranger watched her read it. “Can you do the job?” “Growing them takes longer than the time you’ve given me.” “I know.” “Then what does Pell expect me to deliver?” “Twelve lines your people can plant after frost. Seed from these, not just leaves.” Mara closed her hand around the seeds. “Who are you?” “Someone who took them out of a Helixor vault.” That night Mara ran fragments from the packet through the battered cycler. The machine clicked and steamed. She slept beside it with her coat over her knees, waking whenever it fell silent. In the morning, the results were faint but legible. The old seed carried pieces of the traits Helixor had leased to farms across the continent: cold tolerance, fast growth, resistance to the blight that still stained the greenhouse glass. Some fragments had broken down in storage. Others were intact. And beside them was a sequence Mara had seen in every commercial crop she’d tested. It did no harm to the parent plant. In the next generation, it ruined the seed. She ran the test again. The stranger waited outside, sitting on the bus steps with her empty pistol across her lap. “You knew,” Mara said when she came out. “I hoped I was wrong.” “Your mother stock is Helixor stock.” The stranger’s face changed, though only a little. “The vault inventory said it predated the lock.” “The packet might. These seeds don’t.” Mara sat beside her. “Pell’s offering to pay me with another lot like this?” “He has one that grows true. I saw it.” “Then why does he need twelve more?” “He’s selling them east. One seed lot won’t feed all his buyers.” Mara looked toward the greenhouse. The children had piled the stripped leaves into baskets. Even the yellow ones would go into soup. Three winters earlier, Mara had dosed herself with an untested repair treatment after a glass shard pierced her lung. It had closed the wound. It had also left a web of hard tissue along her ribs that tightened whenever the air turned cold. She pressed a hand there now and felt the familiar catch as she breathed in. The treatment had changed her in one useful way. She could smell mold before it showed on a dish, a sour-metal note so sharp she could pick a contaminated tray out of a row. She had saved whole planting beds that way. She still would have preferred an ordinary lung. “There’s no time to make twelve lines,” she told the stranger. “Not safely. I can start them. I can find out which plants might hold their traits in the next seed. That’s what he gets before frost.” “He’ll say you broke the contract.” “Pell knew what he was asking. Let him explain how twelve harvest-tested lines were supposed to appear in six weeks.” The stranger stood. “And the seed lot?” “We take payment first.” At noon, Pell came in person, riding a motorbike that burned cooking oil. He left it idling outside the bus. Mara showed him twelve labeled trays beneath the grow lamps, each holding a cluster of new green leaves. He barely glanced at them. “Where are the seeds?” “Not grown yet.” “Then the contract isn’t filled.” “The contract says viable lines. They’re alive. If you meant proven seed, you should have brought me the source last spring.” Pell smiled without warmth. “I can take my packet back.” Mara opened one of the Helixor canisters and set it on the bench between them. Inside lay the tested samples, sealed and labeled. “You can. But your eastern buyers will want to know why their harvests fail the following year.” He stared at the canister. “You tested them.” “Twice.” For a long moment, the only sound was the refrigerator compressor rattling under the bench. Pell reached into his coat and brought out a small tin. He put it beside the canister. “The payment lot. Test it too.” “I will.” “And if it’s good?” Mara looked past him at the children carrying their baskets home. “You can have cuttings from the twelve plants when they’re strong enough. Settlement Nine keeps the plants and whatever seed they make. Any buyer of yours gets told what the tests found.” “That wasn’t our deal.” “No,” Mara said. “It’s the one I can keep.” Pell took his hand off the tin. Outside, his motorbike sputtered and died. By evening, Mara had opened the payment lot. The seeds inside were small and pale, with no company stamp on the paper around them. She put the first few in a damp tray and carried the rest to cold storage. They would have to grow before she could trust them. She knew that now better than anyone. In the greenhouse, someone had set a bowl of cabbage soup by her stool. Mara ate while she watched the twelve trays under their lamps. Beyond the glass, frost silvered the empty fields.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This biopunk story successfully creates a compelling post-apocalyptic world centered around genetic engineering and corporate exploitation. The author demonstrates strong adherence to the prompt, incorporating all requested elements: the corporate genetic obsolescence concept, biohacker protagonist, salvaged lab equipment, physical toll of genetic modifications, and a black market contract driving the plot. The worldbuilding is particularly effective, with vivid details like the bicycle-chain-driven centrifuge, the thermal cycler judged by clicking sounds, and the repurposed Helixor canisters serving as constant reminders of corporate dominance. The concept of "licensed continuity" - crops designed to fail after one generation - is both scientifically plausible and thematically resonant. Mara emerges as a well-developed protagonist with clear expertise, moral complexity, and personal stakes. Her lung modification backstory provides both character depth and demonstrates the story's themes about untested genetic treatments. The supporting characters, particularly the unnamed stranger and Pell, serve their narrative functions effectively without feeling like mere plot devices. The dialogue is naturalistic and serves multiple purposes - advancing plot, revealing character, and building tension. Conversations feel authentic to the world and characters, particularly the negotiation scenes that showcase Mara's pragmatic intelligence. The prose strikes an appropriate balance between technical detail and accessibility. Scientific concepts are woven naturally into the narrative without overwhelming lay readers. The writing maintains consistent tone throughout - gritty but not gratuitously dark, technical but not dry. The story's structure builds tension effectively through the contract negotiation, testing sequences, and final confrontation. The resolution feels earned rather than convenient, with Mara using her knowledge and leverage to achieve a realistic compromise rather than a complete victory. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where exposition could be more seamlessly integrated, and the ending, while satisfying, doesn't quite achieve the emotional resonance the setup promises. The story also relies somewhat heavily on familiar post-apocalyptic tropes, though it executes them competently. + Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 82.2
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The transfer vessel’s air filtration system hums with a persistent mechanical drone. Arthur Neegan had repaired enough filters to know that this one was due for a new bearing. Ordinarily he would have found the noise irritating. Now it gave him something smaller than his predicament to think about. Through the porthole, Mars diminished to a rust-colored disk. Somewhere on its night side stood his house, his drilling rig, and the patch of stony ground on which he had intended to spend the rest of his life. Six hours earlier, three armored vehicles had come across that ground without raising a dust plume. Their tires were shrouded; their engines were quiet. Arthur had watched them from his kitchen window while the kettle boiled. The woman who knocked wore a gray uniform and a silver insignia: seven stars arranged around a narrow spear. Antares Diplomatic Corps. “Engineer Neegan,” she had said, “we request the pleasure of your company.” Behind her stood four people carrying compact rifles. “Does your corps know what ‘request’ means?” Arthur had asked. “It does, sir. That is why I’m making one.” He had glanced at the rifles. “It’s also why I hope you’ll agree.” Now she sat across from him in the transfer vessel, reading a paper book. “You can tell me your name,” Arthur said. She closed the book on one finger. “Commander Vale.” “Is that diplomatic?” “It is when someone asks politely.” “Who am I meeting?” “I was instructed to let that person introduce himself.” Arthur looked past her at the stars. “I own eighty hectares of basalt. Last month the surveyors told me something under it might be worth a few billion credits. Yesterday a drone photographed my breakfast. Today you’ve taken me off the planet. I’d like a better answer.” Vale considered him. “The surveyors were mistaken.” “About the value?” “About where the vein ends.” The vessel’s engine note changed. Through the porthole appeared a station: a wheel of habitation modules around a dark central spindle. It carried no flag. “Where are we?” “At a place that is not on any public route,” Vale said. “You may find that useful.” Aboard the station, a narrow corridor led to a room furnished with a desk, three chairs, and a large illuminated map of Mars. Someone had marked the mining districts in white and the corporate lease territories in blue. Arthur’s plot was a red square so small he could cover it with his thumb. A man rose from behind the desk. He was old, with a careful posture and a left hand that trembled until he rested it on the wood. “Mr. Neegan. I’m Elias Thorne.” “The director of Antares?” “Former director. Please sit.” Arthur remained standing. “Am I free to leave?” “Yes,” Thorne said. “Vale will take you home if you ask. But first I hope you’ll hear my offer.” On the map, the red square expanded into a three-dimensional survey. A luminous seam plunged beneath Arthur’s land and continued well beyond it. “The companies think you have an unusually rich deposit,” Thorne said. “In fact, your shaft is the nearest accessible point to a structure some two hundred kilometers long.” Arthur stepped closer. “My equipment couldn’t have resolved that.” “It didn’t. We used a neutrino array.” “Who is ‘we’?” “That is one of the things I’m offering to tell you.” Arthur gave him a sour look. Thorne touched the map. The blue lease territories vanished, replaced by clusters of tiny numbers. “People,” Thorne said. “Indentured workers, counted by housing unit. Their leases are traded between corporations as readily as ore rights. Most signed for passage to Mars. Few have earned enough to buy passage away.” “I know what the leases are. I’ve repaired their pumps.” “Then you know a mining company cannot be trusted to investigate Azra safely.” Arthur folded his arms. “And a diplomat can?” “No. That is why I need an engineer.” Thorne dimmed the map. A second image appeared: a drive chamber, its shielding split open. “Azra hastens radioactive decay,” he said. “Every schoolchild knows the phrase now. What they do not know is that we have seen the effect reach beyond the ore itself. Under certain conditions, nearby material begins to behave like Azra. The chamber failed three weeks ago. We have not established why the reaction stopped.” “How many died?” “Eleven.” “And you came to me because my shaft is close to the vein?” “Because you haven’t sold it. Once a corporation holds that access, its laboratories will race every government laboratory to the answer. Drives are one prospect. Weapons are another. They’ll call the first tests essential, and the casualties regrettable.” Arthur studied the shattered chamber. He knew enough about containment to see where its designers had been confident. “What’s your offer?” “Place your mineral rights in an independent trust. I’ll provide legal protection, equipment, and an inspection team you choose. You’ll direct the work on your land. We will publish findings as soon as they can be verified without giving anyone instructions for making that chamber fail again.” “That’s a great deal of faith to put in one man.” “It’s a great deal of land to put in one man’s name.” Arthur turned to him. “You’ve been the Antares director. You could have asked the colonial council to do this.” “I did. The council chairman’s office sent a copy of my proposal to Helion Mining before I got back to my hotel.” “Then why should I trust you?” Thorne did not answer at once. “You shouldn’t. Read the agreement. Bring your own lawyer. Ask Commander Vale what happened to my last investigation.” Vale, by the door, said, “They stripped him of his post. Two of our surveyors are still missing.” Arthur looked from one to the other. “Yet you’re still wearing their insignia.” “Old uniforms are useful,” Vale said. “People expect us to do what we did at your house.” Thorne brought back the map. Around the red square, new lines appeared: proposed routes for tunnels driven from the neighboring leases. Several had been filed that morning. Arthur recognized a line approaching his eastern boundary. “They’ll come through whether I agree or not.” “They may try.” “And if I agree with you, you’ll try to stop them.” “With inspectors at the shaft and the evidence in public view, yes.” Arthur pictured the miners at the neighboring camp. Some had children who had never seen Earth; all of them lived on ground the companies considered temporary. A tunnel driven in haste could break into his workings while people were still down there. “Send me the agreement,” he said. “And the full chamber report.” Thorne nodded, but Arthur held up a hand. “I haven’t said yes. First I’m going home. I’ll look at what you’ve got, and I’ll talk to the people whose tunnels meet mine.” “The companies won’t welcome that.” “They can tell me so themselves.” For the first time, Thorne smiled. “I believe they will.” On the map, Arthur’s small red square remained amid the blue territories. He had spent twenty years keeping water out of the rock beneath it. By morning, he would have to decide who could be allowed inside.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Asimov style and prompt requirements. The author successfully captures the classic sci-fi atmosphere with clean, functional prose that prioritizes clarity over ornamentation. The dialogue-heavy structure works well, with natural exchanges that reveal character and advance plot simultaneously. The worldbuilding is particularly effective, showing both the intimate details (Arthur's knowledge of air filtration systems) and the larger political machinations (corporate lease territories, indentured workers, interplanetary politics). This mirrors Asimov's trademark approach of grounding cosmic concepts in human-scale concerns. Character development is nuanced throughout. Arthur emerges as a competent, cautious engineer who thinks practically about complex situations. His responses feel authentic - neither naive nor cynically worldly, but appropriately wary. Thorne presents as a believable fallen bureaucrat with genuine concerns, while Vale maintains professional distance that hints at deeper loyalties. The pacing builds tension effectively through revelation rather than action. The gradual unveiling of the Azra vein's true scope, the failed drive chamber, and the political implications creates mounting stakes without melodrama. The technical details about mining, containment, and radioactive decay feel researched and plausible. The prose maintains consistent tone throughout - measured, slightly formal, befitting both the genre conventions and Arthur's engineering mindset. Descriptions serve function over beauty, which suits the material. The imagery of Mars shrinking to a rust-colored disk and the mapping sequences provide effective visual anchors. Some minor weaknesses include occasional exposition that feels slightly mechanical, and the political setup, while competent, follows familiar patterns of corporate malfeasance and government corruption. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness. The ending strikes an appropriate note of uncertainty and impending decision, avoiding false resolution while providing clear forward momentum. Arthur's final contemplation about "who could be allowed inside" effectively encapsulates both the literal mining concerns and the broader trust issues at stake. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 85.9
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
By eleven, the darkroom had reduced the world to three trays, one ticking timer, and Elliot’s reflection in the black window above the sink. He was holding our newest print by its corners, waiting for an image to surface. In the red safelight, his rings looked black. So did the lace cuffs peeking from the sleeves of his thrifted suit jacket. He wore that jacket with combat boots and a pearl earring, as if he’d raided three strangers’ closets and somehow come out looking entirely himself. I’d spent most of the semester trying not to stare. “Too much contrast?” he asked. “Maybe.” I stepped beside him. The image emerged: a chair draped in silver fabric, its shadow falling across the floor like a second, darker chair. “Actually, no. It’s doing something weird. Keep it.” He smiled without looking at me. Elliot had a way of being pleased quietly, like he didn’t want to interrupt anyone else. Our final project was called *Where a Body Might Be*. My title, his photographs. Or that was how I’d described it at first, before he pointed out that arranging the objects was as much part of the picture as pressing the shutter. He was right. I’d been embarrassed by how quickly I’d assigned us roles. I was used to being the person with a plan. At twenty-five, back in school after four years of working jobs that weren’t art, I knew how to claim a worktable and make a decision before a roomful of people talked it to death. Elliot was nineteen, the youngest in our class, and spoke so softly that people sometimes answered over him. I’d done it once. He’d waited, then finished his sentence, and I’d felt like an ass for a week. He lowered the print into the stop bath. “Can I tell you something?” he asked. The timer clicked. Water ran somewhere beyond the wall. “Yeah,” I said. “Of course.” He moved the print gently with the tongs. “I’m not sure I like the title because of the chair.” I waited. It took effort. “It’s more that I keep thinking about the body that’s supposed to be there.” He glanced at me. “Mine, maybe.” I leaned back against the counter. “Okay.” He gave a breath of a laugh. “That sounded less dramatic in my head.” “You don’t owe me dramatic.” “I’ve been questioning some things. About gender.” His gaze went to the trays. “Not exactly new things. Just things I’ve got tired of pretending I’m not questioning.” The room felt suddenly smaller, though neither of us had moved. I thought of every time I’d admired him: the earring, the careful eye makeup, the composure it must take to walk through the art building dressed like that and still raise your hand to ask about aperture. I had treated those details as evidence of a person I understood. Clearly I didn’t. “Thanks for telling me,” I said. Then, because it mattered, “Is there anything you want me to do differently?” “Not right now. He is still fine. I don’t know if it always will be.” “Okay.” “I thought I’d know more by now,” he said. “At nineteen?” “At any age.” I almost told him that twenty-five didn’t come with instructions either. It would have been true, but this wasn’t my turn to be reassuring by making myself the subject. Instead I asked, “Does working on these pictures feel all right?” He considered the print in the fix. “I think so. I didn’t know why I wanted to make them when we started.” I looked at the empty chair under its luminous cloth. For once, I had no useful suggestion about cropping. Elliot lifted the print and carried it to the wash. “You’re being very careful,” he said. “Am I?” “You usually have six opinions by now.” “I still do.” “Let’s hear one.” I crossed my arms. “I think the photograph is good. And I think I’m trying not to say something stupid.” “That’s two.” “The other four are about your jacket.” He laughed, startled enough that I grinned. The attraction I’d kept tucked beneath critiques and coffee runs rose up, inconveniently alive. I’d dated people whose confidence I could recognize across a room—women with sharp edges, men who knew exactly how they wanted to be seen. With Elliot, I kept discovering that my first impression was incomplete. I wanted to know him better. I also wanted him to have room to find out who he was without my expectations crowding him. “I like this one,” he said, setting the washed print on the rack. “Can we do another?” “Absolutely.” I reached for the stack of paper as he adjusted the enlarger. Then the darkroom door swung open. “Sorry!” someone called from the hall. White light cut across the counter before the door slammed shut. For a second, Elliot and I stood still. “The paper,” I said. The top of the stack glowed pale beneath my hand. I checked the box, though I already knew: I’d left it open after taking out the last sheet. Every sheet inside had been exposed. “Oh, hell.” I closed the box. “We can use the other pack,” Elliot said. “We used the last of it.” The student in the hall apologized again through the door. I told them it was okay, though my face felt hot. We had one good print and an unfinished sequence, and I was the one who’d ruined the paper. Elliot pulled up the stool beside mine. “We have the negatives. We can come back tomorrow.” “I know. I just wanted to get it done tonight.” “I did too.” He looked at the box in my hands. “You don’t have to fix it this minute.” I set it down. He was right, which was irritating, and kind. We sat while the wash ran. Without a print to watch, I became aware of how close our knees were. I could have made a joke, or moved away, or taken charge of tomorrow’s schedule. Instead I asked, “Do you want me to keep asking how things are going? With what you told me? Or would you rather bring it up yourself?” “Ask sometimes,” he said. “Just don’t make every conversation about it.” “I can do that.” “And you can still tell me if the contrast is wrong.” “That,” I said, “I might not be able to stop.” His knee touched mine. Neither of us moved. In the red light, he turned toward me, shy and unmistakably curious. I didn’t know what would happen after we finished the photographs, or what either of us would call it. For once, I was willing to wait and see what developed.

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and emotional intelligence in handling a delicate subject matter. The narrative successfully captures Dani's perspective as requested, maintaining her assertive personality while showing how it's complicated by the intimate situation with Elliot. The darkroom setting is used effectively both literally and metaphorically, creating an appropriately confessional atmosphere. The characterization is particularly strong. Dani feels authentic as a 25-year-old returning student - confident but not infallible, attracted to Elliot but genuinely trying to navigate the situation respectfully. Her internal struggle between her natural take-charge tendencies and her desire to give Elliot agency comes through clearly without being heavy-handed. Elliot is portrayed with nuance - vulnerable but not fragile, thoughtful and articulate about his experience. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes: advancing the plot, revealing character, and building intimacy. The conversation about gender identity is handled with sensitivity, avoiding both clinical detachment and overwrought emotion. The pacing allows for natural pauses and reactions. The prose is clean and evocative without being purple. Details like "his rings looked black" and "lace cuffs peeking from the sleeves" efficiently establish atmosphere and character. The photography metaphors are well-integrated rather than forced. The story structure works well, using the ruined paper as a plot device that creates a natural pause and transition. The ending strikes an appropriate note - tentative but hopeful, acknowledging uncertainty while suggesting possibility. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the internal monologue could be more distinctive to Dani's voice, and the attraction element could be developed slightly more to fully satisfy the prompt's emphasis on Dani's "complex attraction." However, these are relatively minor issues in an otherwise accomplished piece. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 80.9
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
At nine in the morning, Ben stepped backward out of an alley near the Trevi Fountain and into the path of a motorcycle. A horn barked. Tires scraped over cobblestones. The motorcycle stopped so close to his knees that he could read the delivery address taped to its handlebars. “Ma sei matto?” The rider lifted her visor. Dark eyes, dark curls escaping her helmet. “Do you study the city, or do you plan to die inside it?” “I’m terribly sorry.” Ben flattened his guidebook against his chest. “I was looking for the fountain.” “It’s the enormous noise behind you.” “Yes. I see that now. Scusi. Sono molto—” “Late?” she supplied. “So am I.” He moved aside. She might have gone then, but her gaze caught on the page he’d been reading. “‘The authentic Rome in one afternoon,’” she read aloud. “That’s a terrible book.” “It’s not research. I teach ancient history. I’m on sabbatical.” “Worse. You should know better.” Ben ought to have been offended. Instead, to his surprise, he laughed. She looked briefly pleased, then covered it by revving the engine. On the side of the motorcycle, beneath the courier company’s neat black lettering, ran a dent painted over in stripes of pink, green, and gold. “What happened to your bike?” he asked. “A disagreement about right of way.” She lowered her visor halfway. “I won.” She rode off, leaving Ben in the alley with the guidebook still open to a map he no longer trusted. *** He found her again twenty minutes later, arguing with a man outside a café. “The package is for Signora Conti,” she told him. “If you are Signora Conti, congratulations on a remarkable disguise.” The man retreated inside. Alessandra turned and saw Ben waiting for coffee at the counter. “Still alive,” she said. “Entirely by your generosity.” “You can thank me by throwing away that book.” “I’ve written notes in it.” “Tragic.” She leaned over the counter, ordered an espresso, and drank it standing up. When she left, a little silver spoon seemed to leave with her, caught between the fingers she used to tug on her glove. Ben glanced at the saucer. By the time he looked back, her hand was empty. “You follow me?” she asked. “I was going to ask you the same.” “This is Rome. We keep running into people.” She inspected his sensible shoes. “Some more slowly than others.” Ben looked at his watch. He had planned a morning in an archive, an afternoon of reading, and dinner alone. None of it required him to answer when she said, “Come on, then. I’ll show you a better fountain.” *** Alessandra kept a spare helmet under the motorcycle seat. Ben held it as though it might explode. “I have a delivery in Testaccio,” she said. “You can come as far as that.” “Is it legal for me to ride on the back?” “Yes.” “Is that your professional opinion?” “No. Put on the helmet.” They left the traffic around Piazza Venezia behind and crossed the city in a rush of sunlight, exhaust, and glimpses Ben couldn’t have found again on a map. He gripped the rail behind him until Alessandra braked at a light. “You’ll fall off doing that,” she said. “I’m trying not to hold on to you.” “I noticed.” The light changed. After one startled second, he put his hands at her waist. At a bakery in Testaccio, she delivered an envelope and talked Ben into a slice of pizza bianca. She paid for his without asking. He tried to reimburse her; she folded his offered coins back into his palm. “You can buy lunch,” she said. “I thought this was lunch.” “Then you’d better keep up.” *** By midday, Ben had seen a courtyard where laundry hung between lemon trees, a view of the river from a street with no tourists, and the Protestant Cemetery, where Alessandra waited while he read a headstone twice. “You like the dead better than the living?” she asked. “They interrupt less.” “I’m interrupting.” “Yes,” he said. “Rather successfully.” She took that in with a tilt of her head. At the gate, a bright blue pencil appeared in her hand. She twirled it once, then tucked it behind her ear. Ben could not remember seeing her pick it up. They ate lunch standing in the shade: supplì too hot to touch, paper napkins turning translucent with oil. Alessandra told him her mother called three times a day if she failed to answer the first call. Ben told her his colleagues believed he was in Rome writing a book. “And are you?” “I’ve written two paragraphs.” “About what?” He considered lying. “Why old roads matter to people who don’t use them anymore.” She stared at him. “That sounds lonely.” “It sounded better in the proposal.” Her phone buzzed. A delivery. The pause between them disappeared as she checked the address. “You’ve lost your guide,” she said. “I never hired one.” “Good. I would have charged too much.” *** At five, she found him sitting on a low wall on the Aventine, his guidebook closed beside him. “You came here yourself?” she asked. “I followed your directions.” “I gave you none.” “You said the hill had a better view. I found the hill.” She laughed and sat beside him. Below, Rome stretched pale and crowded beneath the afternoon haze. Ben had spent the hours since lunch trying to read at his apartment. Every passing motorcycle had brought him to the window. “Did you finish your work?” Alessandra asked. “No.” “Terrible influence, me.” “You seem comfortable with it.” She pulled a narrow red ribbon from her jacket pocket and tied it around the guidebook’s spine. “Where did that come from?” he asked. “Rome.” She stood before he could press her. “Come on. One more place.” *** At dusk they climbed to the Gianicolo. Alessandra had parked below, and Ben, breathless from the steps, accused her of designing the route to humiliate him. “You’re doing fine,” she said. “You could say that with less delight.” From the terrace, the city looked almost still. They stood close enough that his sleeve brushed hers. This time she did not move away. “My flight is on Thursday,” he said. “Today is Monday.” “I know.” “Then why are you worrying about Thursday?” It was a fair question, and one he was beginning to suspect she would never answer for him. At the motorcycle, she put on her helmet and handed him the spare. He hesitated. “I thought the tour was over.” “It is.” “And this?” “I’m taking you home, professore.” Ben looked at the ribbon on his book, at the bright scar on her motorcycle, at the woman waiting with one boot planted impatiently on the road. “Alessandra,” he said, “my apartment is the other way.” “I know.” He put on the helmet anyway.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and adherence to the prompt's requirements. The author successfully creates the requested interconnected scenes spanning a day in Rome, featuring the cultural clash between Alessandra, the fiery Italian courier, and Ben, the polite British academic. The narrative structure works well, using asterisks to separate scenes while maintaining narrative flow. The characterization is particularly effective. Alessandra emerges as a compelling figure - her kleptomania is subtly woven throughout (the spoon, the pencil, the ribbon) without being explicitly stated, exactly as requested. Ben's transformation from guidebook-clutching tourist to someone willing to abandon his planned route feels organic and well-paced. The prose style is clean and economical, avoiding purple prose while still creating vivid scenes. Lines like "At nine in the morning, Ben stepped backward out of an alley near the Trevi Fountain and into the path of a motorcycle" immediately establish tension and place. The author shows rather than tells throughout most of the piece, letting character actions and dialogue reveal personality and attraction. The Rome setting feels authentic rather than touristy, moving beyond obvious landmarks to places like Testaccio and the Protestant Cemetery. The motorcycle serves as both practical transport and metaphor for the journey Ben is taking outside his comfort zone. However, the piece has some limitations. While competently executed, it doesn't take significant creative risks or offer particularly surprising moments. The attraction between the characters, while believable, follows fairly predictable romantic comedy beats. The ending, while satisfying, doesn't provide the "payoff" mentioned in the prompt as strongly as it could have. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 82.2
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
By the second hour of evening shift, the Last Outpost smells of fried onions, machine oil, and whatever Captain Orra insists is cinnamon. The mining crew has claimed the tables nearest the heaters. Two merchants are playing cards on an upside-down cargo crate. Through the window, the belt turns slowly past, all dark stone and pinpricks of navigation light. This is the hour when people tell me things they won’t tell each other. “Nets,” Orra says, leaning over the bar, “tell Pell that borrowing a shuttle and returning a shuttle with the same *number* of engines are different things.” Pell, three stools down, raises his mug. “The remaining engine works beautifully.” “It whistles.” “It’s cheerful.” “It whistles in vacuum.” I slide Orra her tea. “You did say he could borrow it.” “I said he could move it.” “See?” Pell says. “From berth six to berth seven,” Orra adds. “Details,” Pell says, and I put another kettle on. They have been having this argument for four days. Neither has asked me to settle it, which is fortunate, because I was the one who told Pell the shuttle might survive the trip. I have other talents. The hatch sighs open. A stranger steps in, tentacled dreads askew, coat half-fastened, eyes fixed on the bar as if crossing the room requires all their concentration. They take the empty stool at the far end. “Vega whisky, neat,” they say quietly. “Better make that a double.” I set out a glass. “Long crossing?” “Short one. Felt long.” The whisky splashes amber against the glass. They look at it but don’t drink. “Dock seven’s yours?” I ask. They nod. “Then you should know the air recycler on that side hums. We tell guests it’s music.” “I’m not staying.” “That’s what most guests say.” They finally take a sip. One of their dreads curls around a wrist, then lets go. Across the room, Pell is explaining why a borrowed engine ought to count as a gift if its owner doesn’t want it back. The stranger says, “Are you Nettle?” “Depends who’s asking.” “Someone hoping you’ll deny it.” “That narrows it down less than you’d think.” They pull a folded document from their coat and lay it between us. The top line reads **NOTICE OF CLAIM: ANCHORAGE NINETEEN**. I know our anchorage number. I wish I didn’t. Behind me, somewhere near the dish return, a glass accidentally breaks. Juno calls, “My fault! Nobody move,” and goes for the broom. Orra and Pell stop arguing long enough to lift their feet. The stranger watches my face. “You know what this is.” “I know the heading.” “Northstar Salvage filed it this morning. Their tug arrives at first light.” “Northstar doesn’t own the Outpost.” “According to the registry, there is no Outpost. There’s an abandoned service platform attached to a mineral lease.” I read the next line. “They’re claiming the docking ring?” “And everything connected to it.” That includes the bar, the heaters, Juno’s little galley, and Pell’s favorite place to avoid telling Orra what happened to her shuttle. “What’s your name?” I ask. “Rell.” “You work for Northstar?” “I route their tugs.” “Why are you telling me this?” Rell turns the document around. At the bottom is a survey certification, thirteen years old. My name is on it. Not Nettle. The other one. *Surveyor I. Venn.* For a moment the bar is all noise: the recycler, Orra’s voice, the tiny bells Juno hung over the galley door. I hold the edge of the paper so my hand has somewhere to be. “That survey covers half the belt,” I say. “It lists this anchorage as unoccupied.” “It was an inventory of registered structures.” “I know. I looked it up.” “There was no beacon here then.” “There was a platform.” “There were hundreds of platforms.” Rell’s expression softens, which is worse than anger. “I didn’t come to argue about what you could have seen.” “Then why come?” “Because Northstar found your survey. They’re using it as the basis for an uncontested salvage claim. And because the woman on the certification might know how to stop them.” I pour Rell a water without asking. They drink it in one swallow. At the other end of the bar, Orra says, “Nets? Everything all right?” “No,” I say. That gets everyone’s attention. I usually have a better answer ready. Pell swivels on his stool. “Is it my tab?” “Not tonight.” I lay the notice flat. “Northstar says we’re abandoned.” Orra comes over and reads it. “I’ve been eating breakfast here for eleven years.” “Registry doesn’t accept breakfast as evidence of occupation,” Rell says. “It ought to.” “I agree.” Juno arrives with the broom in hand. “My grandmother welded the galley wall. Would that help?” “Maybe,” I say. “If we can prove when.” Orra scans the signature. Her eyes move from the paper to me. She says nothing for a long enough moment that I would welcome another broken glass. “You did survey work,” she says at last. “Yes.” “You never mentioned Northstar.” “It wasn’t Northstar then.” “That’s not what I asked.” “I know.” Pell leans in. “Can you amend it?” “Not in the current registry. The appeal desk opens after the tug’s scheduled arrival.” “Convenient,” Orra says. Rell taps the notice. “They’ll secure the ring before they tow anything. There’s time to object while they work, if you have proof.” “How much time?” Juno asks. “Hours. Possibly less if nobody makes them slow down.” Pell gives Orra a hopeful look. “I can make a tug slow down.” “No,” Orra and I say together. He sighs. “You both dismiss my skills.” “I know exactly what your skills are,” Orra says. “That’s why I’m saying no.” Juno braces her broom against the counter. “Grandmother kept receipts. She kept receipts for gifts.” “Where?” I ask. “In the galley, the storeroom, her cabin. Possibly inside the cooker.” “Start with her cabin.” Orra folds her arms. “I’ve got the old berth log. It’s paper. Let the registry try to delete that.” Rell says, “Northstar will call private logs unverifiable.” “Then they can say it to my face.” I reach for the notice again. My old signature sits beneath a neat, terrible word: *unoccupied*. “Why did you bring this to me?” I ask Rell. They glance toward the window. Far out among the rocks, a tug’s running lights move against the stars—too distant to be ours, too bright to ignore. “Because when dispatch sent the claim through,” Rell says, “the tug captain asked why your name was on it.” “Who’s the captain?” Rell gathers their empty glass in both hands. “Your former supervisor.” Orra sets down the berth log she has fetched from under the counter. Nobody speaks. Even Pell seems to understand that his engine can wait. I look at the log, then at my signature. “Juno, put another kettle on.” “It’s already on.” “Good.” I turn to Rell. “Tell us everything you know about that tug.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the cozy sci-fi atmosphere requested. The author successfully establishes the setting of The Last Outpost as a lived-in, comfortable space where regulars engage in familiar banter about borrowed shuttles and broken engines. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - revealing character relationships, providing exposition, and maintaining the light tone even as serious conflict emerges. The central conflict is well-constructed: Nettle's past as surveyor I. Venn has created a legal vulnerability that threatens the community she's found refuge in. The revelation unfolds organically through Rell's arrival and the salvage notice, creating genuine stakes without resorting to melodrama. The author skillfully balances the cozy atmosphere with mounting tension, particularly effective in moments like Orra's pointed questioning about Nettle's past with Northstar. Character work is nuanced throughout. Nettle emerges as someone competent but carrying secrets, while the supporting cast feels authentic - Pell's cheerful destructiveness, Orra's protective pragmatism, and Juno's earnest helpfulness all ring true. Rell serves as an effective catalyst, bringing bad news while showing reluctant sympathy for the Outpost's residents. The prose maintains consistent quality with economical but evocative descriptions. Lines like "the belt turns slowly past, all dark stone and pinpricks of navigation light" establish the setting without overwrought detail. The author shows restraint in world-building, providing just enough sci-fi elements to feel authentic without overwhelming the intimate bar setting. The dialogue percentage meets the requested 60% and feels natural throughout. Conversations flow believably, from the ongoing shuttle argument to the more serious exchanges about the salvage claim. The author avoids exposition dumps, instead weaving necessary information into character interactions. The chapter ends on an appropriate cliffhanger with the revelation of Nettle's "former supervisor" as the tug captain, escalating personal stakes while leaving resolution for future chapters as requested. The pacing builds steadily from comfortable routine to mounting crisis without feeling rushed. Minor weaknesses include some predictable elements in the setup and a few moments where the dialogue could be tighter, but these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness of the piece. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The man who drove me into New Orleans leaves me outside a pharmacy at 6:12 in the morning. “End of the line,” he says, which seems unfair because I never saw a line, only his truck’s cracked windshield and the back of his head. I shoulder my backpack. He pulls away before I can thank him or decide whether I want to. The city smells like rain on hot concrete, coffee, and something sweet going rotten. A streetcar rattles past. I have forty-three dollars, a phone at nine percent, and no idea where I am except *not Tennessee*. For about six seconds, that feels like freedom. Then I need a bathroom. Inside the pharmacy, a woman in a purple visor points me toward the back without making me buy anything. I wash my face in the sink and stare at myself under the lights. Same nose. Same split in my lower lip from biting it too hard yesterday. On the mirror, somebody has stuck a tiny silver star. Two days ago, I told my family I’m trans. Mom cried like I’d announced a terminal illness. Dad asked if the school counselor had put the idea in my head. I’d spent years wanting them to ask me who I was; when they finally did, nobody listened to the answer. My phone lights up: **Mom: Please tell me you’re safe.** I type *I am* and delete it. I don’t know if it’s true yet. Outside, I buy the cheapest bottle of water I can find. I walk because standing still makes me feel like I’ve made a mistake, and moving lets me postpone deciding. By late morning, I’m on a crowded street where balconies drip ferns overhead and a saxophone cuts through everybody’s conversations. The musician is playing something slow, full of notes that almost sound like words. I stop beside a shop window displaying masks with gold feathers. “Tourist?” someone asks. A girl about my age stands next to me with a paper bag under one arm. Her black eyeliner has survived the heat better than the rest of her. “Do I look like one?” “You look like you’re waiting for the street to tell you what to do.” “That obvious?” “Only to me.” She pulls a pastry from the bag and tears it in half. “I’m Jules.” I don’t take the offered half. Yesterday, Dad said I’d have to learn that choices have consequences. Today, everybody seems to have an opinion about what I should do next. “Taylor,” I say. Jules eats her half. “Good. I was going to eat both anyway.” I laugh, despite myself. She grins and points with the remaining pastry. “There’s a place a few blocks over where you can sit down and charge your phone. They give out lunch, too.” “What place?” “A youth center. They helped me when I got here.” “How do I know you’re not leading me somewhere terrible?” “You don’t.” She puts the other half back in the bag and holds it out. “You can look it up. I’ll stand here.” I use the last of my battery checking. The place has a website, a phone number, and pictures of a building with orange doors. When I look up, Jules is watching the saxophonist instead of my screen. “Okay,” I say. “But you walk in front.” “Sure.” The saxophonist starts a faster song as we leave. I can still hear it at the end of the block. *** The center’s doors really are orange. Inside, the air-conditioning makes the sweat on my back go cold. Someone has painted **YOU BELONG HERE** across one wall. I hate how badly I want that to be true. At the front desk, a man named Darnell asks what name I want him to use. Just like that. No startled pause, no speech about how hard this is for other people. “Taylor.” “Glad you’re here, Taylor. You want food first, or a place to sit?” My throat tightens. “Can I charge my phone?” He points to an outlet beside a couch. “All three are possible.” Lunch is rice, beans, and an orange. Jules sits opposite me and peels hers in one long strip. “Do you live here?” I ask. “At the center? No.” She looks down at her hands. “I’ve been sleeping at my aunt’s apartment this week.” “Then why did you say they helped you when you got here?” “Because they did.” I wait. Jules folds the orange peel into a small, damp square. “I ran from home,” she says. “Got here three weeks ago. My aunt came to pick me up two days later. I didn’t know if she would.” “Why did you run?” She studies me for a moment. “My mom’s boyfriend kept taking my money. Money I earned. When I said I was leaving, he told me my aunt wouldn’t want the trouble.” She presses a thumbnail into the peel. “I believed him long enough to spend a night outside.” I look at my backpack on the floor. Last night, I’d been so sure leaving was the one smart thing I’d done. “Does your aunt know you come here?” “Yeah. I meet a counselor. And Darnell makes good rice.” She glances up. “You can still leave if you want to. But you could talk to him first.” My phone reaches five percent and starts buzzing. Mom has called eleven times. There’s one message from my younger brother: **Your room looks weird empty.** A minute later, another: **I didn’t say anything because Dad was there. I heard you.** I cry right there at the table, which is humiliating. Jules slides a napkin toward me and keeps eating her orange. When I can speak, I tell Darnell I left home last night. He asks whether I have somewhere safe to stay tonight. I say no. He tells me we can sit down together and go over my options. He doesn’t make me promise anything first. By evening, I’ve sent Mom a message: **I’m safe right now. I need some time. Please call me Taylor.** The reply doesn’t come immediately. I put my phone face down anyway. Through the window, the street is still crowded. Somewhere beyond it, a saxophone plays a few notes I recognize from this morning. I sit on the couch with Jules at the other end, waiting while Darnell finds the number he said he’d call with me. I don’t know what Mom will say. I don’t know where I’ll sleep tomorrow. But I know the name the man at the desk will call when he comes back, and for now, I’ll answer it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and emotional authenticity in depicting a transgender teenager's first day as a runaway in New Orleans. The writing successfully captures Taylor's voice through a mix of vulnerability, wariness, and tentative hope that feels genuine for a 16-year-old in crisis. The adherence to instructions is excellent - the piece follows Taylor through their first day, introduces Jules as another runaway with her own backstory, maintains first-person mixed tense throughout, and incorporates both internal monologue and dialogue effectively. The 1000-word count is respected. Character development is nuanced and believable. Taylor's actions feel authentic - the mixture of bravado and fear, the careful testing of trust with Jules, the emotional breakdown when reading their brother's message. Jules is well-crafted as a character who has her own agency and secrets without being merely a plot device. The supporting characters like Darnell feel real rather than idealized. The prose is clean and elegant, with strong sensory details that ground the reader in New Orleans without overwhelming the narrative. Lines like "The city smells like rain on hot concrete, coffee, and something sweet going rotten" and the recurring saxophone motif create atmosphere effectively. The emotional complexity is handled well - Taylor experiences conflicting feelings about their escape, their family, and their uncertain future. The piece avoids simple resolution while allowing for measured hope. The ending strikes an appropriate balance, acknowledging Taylor's continued uncertainty while providing some stability. Dialogue feels natural and serves character development. Jules's speech patterns distinguish her from Taylor, and conversations reveal information organically rather than through exposition dumps. The pacing is controlled, moving Taylor through the day without rushing toward false resolution. The youth center provides realistic support without magical solutions. The piece earns its moments of lightness through Taylor's small victories in being recognized and finding temporary safety. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose becomes slightly self-conscious, and the saxophone motif, while effective, borders on being overly symbolic. The piece also relies somewhat on familiar runaway narrative beats, though it executes them well. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 79.8
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The first problem was breakfast. The second problem was that breakfast had been eaten yesterday. Midas stood in the doorway of the old tollbooth, looking out at the rain. Beside him sat Chewy, an animo-tronic stuffed koala with one glass eye, two working fingers, and a voice box from an age when people had considered it helpful for toys to say things without being asked. “Let’s have an adventure!” Chewy announced. “That’s the third problem,” said Midas. They had a little water, half a candle, and seventeen jars of pickled turnip left by the tollbooth’s previous occupants. The jars were not technically empty. Their contents had simply developed opinions. Midas had spent the previous afternoon searching the nearby ruins for anything edible. Instead he’d found a message painted beneath a collapsed flyover: **WHEN THE LAST ROAD ENDS, ASK THE TREES FOR SHELTER. THREE WHITE STONES. ONE RED DOOR.** “It might be a refuge,” he said. “There might be food.” “There might be friends!” said Chewy. “There might be whoever painted it, defending their food.” Chewy’s head clicked to one side. “Let’s have an adventure!” Midas took this for agreement. Chewy had once possessed a broader vocabulary, but a flood had narrowed it considerably. They packed a jar of turnips for emergencies and set off for the last road. This was easy to find. The road ended half a mile north of the tollbooth, where the river had swallowed a bridge. Beyond it lay woodland. Midas knew the bridge was gone because, two weeks earlier, he had walked confidently onto its remains. Today they crossed upstream on a fallen oak. Chewy rode in Midas’s pack, offering encouragement every time Midas’s foot slipped. They found the first white stone by noon. It was the size of a wheel and marked with a faded arrow. The second stood farther in, beside a patch of mushrooms Chewy urged Midas not to eat. His warnings took the form of a jaunty tune; Midas listened anyway. The third stone stood in a clearing. Behind it was a red door. The door had no wall. It was fixed between two posts, with open forest on either side. Midas walked around it. On the back, in fresh paint, someone had written **PLEASE KNOCK**. “That seems unnecessary,” he said. He knocked. A wire tightened under the leaves. Midas felt it brush his ankle a moment before a net lifted him into the air. The pack fell from his shoulder. Chewy landed face down in a puddle. A woman stepped out from behind a tree, carrying a spear and wearing an apron. “Why’d you go around the door?” she asked. “I wanted to see what was behind it.” “And then you knocked?” “It asked.” The woman looked up at him for a while. “Fair enough.” She lowered the net. Her name was Ada, and she belonged to a settlement half a mile away. The door, she explained, was there to help visitors show themselves before they reached the houses. Most people knocked from the front. “I can do that now,” Midas offered. “You’ve made an impression already.” Ada led them to a ring of low buildings sheltered by the trees. Smoke rose from a clay oven. Chickens crossed the path ahead of them, followed by a child assigned to keep them out of the gardens. Midas stopped looking at the chickens and looked at the gardens instead. Ada took them to the settlement’s pump. Its handle moved freely, but the pipe beneath it rattled and delivered only a mouthful of brown water. Their spring had been failing for days. They had food, Ada said, but could spare little until someone fetched water from a seep farther uphill. Midas had come all this way and could not bring himself to leave without helping. He had also noticed that Ada’s apron pockets held fresh bread. “I’ll go,” he said. “There might be friends!” Chewy said from the pack. Ada gave them two buckets and directions. She advised Midas to avoid the old quarry. Naturally, the path to the seep looked shortest through the old quarry. At its edge he paused. A proper path wound away between the trees; the quarry floor lay straight ahead. He chose the quarry, telling himself he could still see the far side. He had nearly reached it when the ground gave way beneath one bucket. The bucket dropped into a shallow pit, and Midas followed, sliding down a bank of loose stone. He landed on his back with Chewy on his chest. Above them, the rim was higher than he could reach. “Let’s have an adventure!” Chewy said into his ear. “I’d prefer a ladder.” Chewy’s remaining eye flashed red, then went dark. His batteries had finally run out. Midas tried calling for help. Nothing answered. He took Chewy off his chest and sat up, feeling along the pit walls for a foothold. His hand found a pipe buried in the bank. It was loose. When he pulled, cold water trickled across his fingers. He dug around it with a flat stone. The pipe led into the quarry wall, where fallen rubble had bent it almost shut. Midas shifted the smaller rocks, then braced his feet and hauled at a larger one until it rolled aside. Water burst from the crushed pipe and filled the bottom of the pit. For one alarming minute, Midas thought he had improved the quarry rather than his circumstances. Then the water carried the empty bucket within reach of the rim. He stood on it, caught a root, and climbed out, dragging Chewy by the strap of his pack. By the time he got back to the settlement, the pit had overflowed into an old drainage channel. Water was running downhill toward the houses. Ada and two others followed him back to the quarry with shovels. They cleared the channel’s mouth, and by evening water was flowing into their holding pond. Ada gave Midas bread, eggs, and dry batteries for Chewy. She offered them a place to stay. Midas thanked her, but he wanted to get back before dark. The tollbooth was damp and short of food, yet their blankets were there, and the roof had survived every storm so far. They crossed the oak at dusk. Midas slipped once, saved the eggs, and soaked himself to the waist. Back at the tollbooth, he set the bread on the table, changed into dry trousers, and fitted Chewy’s new batteries. Chewy blinked. “Welcome home!” he said. Midas lit the half-candle. Outside, the rain began again. He had come home with dinner, a bruised shoulder, and mud in places his clothes ought to have protected. In the morning he would go back and help Ada finish the channel. For tonight, he was content to stay where the roof held. Chewy clicked softly beside him as Midas broke the bread.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This story successfully captures many elements of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style while crafting an engaging post-apocalyptic adventure. The opening lines immediately establish the dry, matter-of-fact tone that characterizes Pratchett's work, with the escalating "problems" format creating both humor and exposition efficiently. The characterization is particularly strong. Midas emerges as a believably flawed protagonist whose curiosity consistently leads him into trouble - from walking around the mysterious door to choosing the obviously dangerous quarry route. His actions feel authentic to his established character rather than forced by plot convenience. Chewy, despite his limited vocabulary, becomes a genuine character through the author's clever use of his mechanical limitations and timing of his phrases. The world-building is subtle but effective, painting a picture of technological collapse through details like the flooded tollbooth, collapsed flyovers, and Chewy's degraded functionality. The prose maintains Pratchett's characteristic blend of whimsy and pragmatism, particularly in descriptions like the pickled turnips that "had simply developed opinions." The story structure follows the requested format well - setup, mission gone sideways, return home worse for wear - while subverting expectations by having the mishap accidentally solve a larger problem. This creates genuine narrative satisfaction rather than mere coincidence. However, the piece has some weaknesses. The dialogue, while functional, lacks the sharp wit and philosophical undertones that make Pratchett's conversations memorable. Ada's character, while serviceable, feels somewhat generic compared to the vivid personalities Pratchett typically creates for even minor characters. The emotional complexity is limited - while the story is engaging, it doesn't explore deeper themes about survival, community, or human nature that might elevate it beyond a competent adventure tale. The ending strikes an appropriate balance between modest success and ongoing hardship, avoiding unearned optimism while providing satisfying closure. The prose flows naturally throughout, maintaining readability without sacrificing the distinctive voice. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell above the bookshop door rang once, sharply, and a man in a dark coat came in sideways. “Shut it,” he said. Efa looked up from the parcel she was tying. “Good afternoon to you too.” “Sorry. Please shut it.” He pressed himself against a shelf of Welsh poetry while Efa crossed to the door. Outside, two photographers hurried past the window toward Conwy’s castle walls. She turned the sign to **AR GAU**. The man let out a breath. “You’ve saved my life.” “I’ve delayed two people with cameras. It’s a narrower service.” He smiled as if she’d said something encouraging. He had the kind of face Efa had seen on bus shelters: handsome from a distance, and, to her annoyance, even better close up. “You know who I am,” he said. “I know you’re leaning on Menna Elfyn.” He stepped away from the shelf. “That sounds like an accusation.” “It’s a signed first edition.” He glanced at the books behind him. “Then I apologise to Ms Elfyn as well.” “Take your time. They’ll come back.” “Is that an invitation?” “It’s a weather forecast.” He laughed. Efa went back behind the counter, where her fingers made a mess of the parcel string. She hid the knot under her palm. “I’m Adrian Voss,” he said. “I gathered.” “And you are?” “Working.” “Working,” he repeated. “Unusual name.” “It was my grandmother’s.” He came toward the counter, still smiling, though he had begun to watch her more carefully. “You must get actors hiding in here all the time.” “Only on wet Thursdays.” “It’s Tuesday.” “Then you’re our first.” His smile faltered for half a second. Efa saw it, and felt meaner than she’d intended. She’d enjoyed him in *A Kingdom of Ash*, even cried at the end, but she wasn’t about to tell him that while he stood in her shop waiting for applause. Outside, a photographer stopped and peered into the tea room opposite. Adrian moved out of sight. “Are they after you for something interesting?” she asked. “Depends what you find interesting.” “That usually means no.” “They photographed me coming out of a hotel with a woman who isn’t my girlfriend.” “Do you have a girlfriend?” “No. Neither does she. We were there for a film meeting.” “That sounds inconvenient for the headline.” “It was.” He looked at her parcel. “You don’t believe me.” “I haven’t decided whether it’s my business.” “Most people decide it is.” Efa loosened the string and started again. “Most people don’t have an order to post before five.” “There it is,” he said softly. “What?” “Someone who doesn’t want anything from me.” She pulled the knot tight. “I want you to stop standing where customers can see you through the window.” Adrian obeyed, taking refuge beside a revolving rack of postcards. “Better?” “Much.” “Anything else?” “You could buy a book.” “Ah. There’s the catch.” He turned the rack once, slowly. Efa should have let the silence stand, but she found herself wondering whether he read on trains, whether he folded corners, whether he remembered anything once someone stopped pointing a camera at him. “What sort?” he asked. “A book you’ll finish.” “That limits us.” “Fiction?” “I spend all day pretending. What else have you got?” She led him to a shelf of local histories. He followed close enough that she could smell rain on his coat. “Conwy: town, castle, river,” she said, handing him a slim paperback. “Pictures, maps, a chapter about the fishing boats. You can learn where you’ve been.” “I know where I’ve been.” “Then you can check whether the author does.” He opened it. “Do you always argue with customers?” “Only the ones who introduce themselves before saying hello.” “I said sorry.” “For the door. Not for the introduction.” Adrian looked up. This time his smile came late and uncertain. Efa liked it better, which was unfortunate. “When I was twelve,” he said, “I played the innkeeper in a school play. Two lines. I forgot the first, so I bowed. Everyone laughed.” He rubbed a thumb along the edge of the book. “I bowed again. They laughed harder.” “Sounds like quick thinking.” “I couldn’t get off the stage afterward. I thought if I stopped making them laugh, they’d remember I’d ruined it.” He closed the book. “I’m afraid I still do that.” Efa’s answer caught somewhere in her throat. Beyond the window, a gull landed on the chimney pots and shook rain from its wings. “You didn’t ruin it,” she said. “You weren’t there.” “No. But they had a good time.” “That’s very generous of you.” “Don’t get used to it.” He smiled at the floor. “Too late.” The bell rattled. Both of them turned. Through the glass, one photographer cupped his hands around his face to look inside. Efa walked to the door and pulled down the narrow blind. “Closed,” she called. “We saw him come in.” “Then you saw me close.” “Adrian! Just a word!” Adrian stayed by the histories. He’d gone still, the book held awkwardly against his chest. “There’s a back door,” Efa told him when the men moved away. “Does it lead to an alley full of photographers?” “It leads to bins. The photographers may arrive later.” He gave a short laugh. “You really will sell me this, won’t you?” “It’s eight pounds.” “I haven’t got cash.” “We take cards.” At the till, their hands met over the paperback. It was barely a touch. Efa looked down at the card reader as if its instructions were complicated. “I’ll finish it,” he said. “You don’t have to promise.” “I know.” He put the book into his coat pocket. “Could I come back and tell you if the author got it right?” “You haven’t been here long enough to know.” “Then I’d better come back and find out.” Efa opened the back door onto a strip of wet cobbles. He paused beside her, waiting, for once, without a smile to help him. “Ask for Efa,” she said. His face brightened. “I thought it was Working.” “That was my grandmother.” He laughed, and went out into the rain.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the requested romantic tension and character dynamics. The author successfully creates two distinct voices - Adrian's performative charm masking insecurity, and Efa's dry Welsh wit serving as both shield and sword. The dialogue crackles with subtext, particularly in exchanges like "I want you to stop standing where customers can see you through the window" / "Anything else?" / "You could buy a book" / "Ah. There's the catch." The Welsh setting feels authentic rather than tourist-brochure superficial, with natural references to Conwy, Welsh poetry (Menna Elfyn), and the bilingual "AR GAU" sign. The bookstore environment is well-realized through specific details like signed first editions and the parcel-tying that gives Efa's hands something to do while she processes her attraction. Character development is particularly strong. Adrian's vulnerability emerges organically through the school play anecdote, which feels like genuine backstory rather than exposition. His line "I'm afraid I still do that" lands with real pathos. Efa's internal conflict between her attraction and her principles creates compelling tension - she's genuinely immune to his practiced charm but drawn to his unguarded moments. The pacing builds naturally from antagonistic banter to tentative connection. The photographers provide external pressure without overwhelming the intimate character work. The ending strikes an appropriate note - hopeful but not overly romantic, with Efa's final joke ("That was my grandmother") showing she's willing to play along while maintaining her wit. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose becomes slightly self-conscious, and the metaphor of Adrian as someone who "couldn't get off the stage" could have been developed more subtly throughout. The piece also relies somewhat heavily on the "gruff local vs. charming outsider" dynamic, though it executes this familiar setup with enough freshness to avoid feeling stale. The dialogue consistently serves multiple purposes - advancing plot, revealing character, and building romantic tension. The author shows admirable restraint in not pushing the attraction too far too fast, allowing the chemistry to simmer rather than boil over.
