+ Noir romance: Carnival of Dangerous Intentions — Score: 80.5
Prompt:
Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
She stopped just before the shooting gallery. The boardwalk’s sodium lights flickered inconsistently, casting strange patterns on strangers’ faces. A woman passing with a paper cone of sugared almonds looked, for an instant, bruised. Then the light steadied and she was simply tired. *His locks.* There it was again, that absurd old phrase. Not his hair, though she remembered that well enough: black curls falling over his forehead when he had bent to pick up her dropped glove. *His locks*, as though she were a girl in a novel, free to consider a man’s appearance and nothing else. Nora could still turn back. Her sister had answered the telephone that afternoon. Elsie was safe, or had been then. Inside the gallery, a rifle cracked. A tin duck pitched backward. “You came,” the young man said. He stood beside the counter in shirtsleeves, his jacket folded over one arm. The lights made his dark eyes difficult to read. “I said I might.” “I heard you say you would.” “You hear what suits you.” “That’s possible.” He did not smile. Nora had liked his smile yesterday, which was reason enough to be wary of it. The gallery attendant slid a rifle toward an impatient boy. Behind him, painted ships rocked on iron rods. Nora moved out of the line of fire, and the stranger moved with her, leaving a careful distance between them. “You frightened me for nothing,” she said. “Is Elsie home?” “She will be.” “That isn’t what I asked.” Nora looked toward the dance pavilion at the far end of the boardwalk. Its roof stood black against the last blue of the sky. Music drifted out each time the doors opened. “You said there might be a fire,” she said. “People say all sorts of things at Coney Island.” “Yes.” “Is there?” “I don’t know.” “Then why did you tell me?” “Because someone paid to have the rear doors chained after the last show.” For a moment the music seemed to recede. Elsie’s shift ended after midnight. She used the rear door because the manager disliked the girls leaving through the front among paying customers. Nora folded her arms. “Who paid?” “That’s what I hope to find out.” “You expected me to bring you the key.” “I hoped you would.” The hotel room key lay in her handbag, warm from her palm. She had taken it from the desk at the Seabright that morning, before her employer noticed that one of his guests had not returned it. Room 414 belonged to a man who seldom slept there and received visitors he never entered in the register. Nora had given the stranger none of this information. Yesterday he had known where she worked. Today he knew about Elsie. She disliked how much she wanted to know what else he knew. “You could go to the police,” she said. “So could you.” “I intend to.” “Then you should.” The ease of his answer unsettled her. “You don’t believe me.” “I believe you’ll try to get your sister out first.” Nora reached into her handbag. His gaze dropped to it, then returned to her face. “If I give you this,” she said, “what happens?” “I go into the room.” “And after?” “I look for a receipt.” “What receipt?” “One that may tell us who ordered the chains. If it’s there, I’ll bring it to you.” “You’ll bring it to the police.” “If that’s still what you want.” A shot rang out. The boy at the counter whooped, and the attendant handed him a small plaster dog. Nora waited until they had both turned away. “You speak as though there might be a reason I wouldn’t.” “There might be a name on it you recognize.” She thought of her employer, who had kept her on when other girls were let go. She thought of the money he lent Elsie last winter, when she was ill. There were names Nora would rather not find on a receipt. She could not let that matter. “You haven’t told me yours,” she said. “Vale.” “First or last?” “Last.” “And the first?” He hesitated. “Daniel.” She had asked because a name could be checked. Now that she had one, she found herself watching his mouth instead of considering where to begin. “Daniel Vale,” she said. “If that’s true.” “It’s true.” “You can’t expect me to take your word.” “No.” He seemed about to say more, but a man in a straw hat stopped at the gallery and called to the attendant. Vale turned his head slightly. Nora followed his glance. The man was buying three shots, nothing more; he did not look at them. “I warned Elsie,” Nora said. “I thought you had.” “She won’t go to work tomorrow.” “I’m glad.” “Tonight she’s still there. Her manager says he’ll dismiss her if she leaves early.” “Can you get word to her?” “I’ve tried. They won’t fetch the girls to the telephone during a show.” Vale looked toward the pavilion. “Then go to her.” “And leave you with the key?” “Yes.” His answer came too quickly. He could enter the room while she crossed the boardwalk; by the time she returned, he might be gone with whatever he found. Yet he was right about Elsie. Nora had delayed coming here because she wanted to see whether he would be waiting. She was ashamed of that small, costly curiosity. She drew out the key. On its brass tag, **414** had been stamped so deeply the numbers showed through on the other side. Vale held out his hand, but Nora closed her fingers over the tag. “If you find anything, you come to the pavilion,” she said. “You tell me before you take it anywhere.” “That may not be wise.” “It’s the bargain I’m offering.” He considered her. Beneath the unreliable light, the curls at his temple shone briefly, then went dark. “All right,” he said. Nora put the key in his hand. His fingers brushed hers as he took it; she could not tell whether he had meant them to. She turned at once toward the pavilion. “Miss Mercer,” he called. She looked back. “There may be someone at the rear doors already. Use the front.” Nora nodded and went on. She had never told him her surname.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric control, successfully creating the requested blend of romantic tension and moral ambiguity set in 1937 Coney Island. The author establishes an effective noir-like atmosphere with careful attention to period details and lighting effects that enhance the sense of danger lurking beneath surface interactions. The dialogue feels natural and period-appropriate, with characters speaking in clipped, careful exchanges that reveal information gradually while maintaining tension. The conversation between Nora and Vale effectively builds suspense through what's left unsaid as much as what's revealed. The author handles the requested dialogue-to-exposition ratio reasonably well, though the internal monologue portions could be more substantial. Character development is nuanced, particularly Nora's internal conflict between self-preservation, concern for her sister, and her inexplicable attraction to Vale. Her moral complexity comes through in her recognition of potentially compromising information while still choosing to act. Vale remains appropriately mysterious while showing enough humanity to make the attraction believable. The prose style successfully evokes the requested "classic sensibility" with restrained elegance. Sentences like "The boardwalk's sodium lights flickered inconsistently, casting strange patterns on strangers' faces" demonstrate strong atmospheric writing without becoming overwrought. The recurring motif of "his locks" effectively ties back to the prompt while showing Nora's internal state. The pacing builds tension effectively, culminating in the key exchange and Vale's knowledge of her surname - a genuinely unsettling revelation that promises future complications. The author avoids easy resolutions while advancing the plot meaningfully. However, some elements feel slightly predictable within the noir genre conventions. The mysterious stranger with dangerous knowledge, the working-class heroine caught between loyalty and desire, and the corrupt establishment figures follow familiar patterns. While executed competently, the story doesn't transcend its genre constraints to offer truly surprising insights. The ending maintains appropriate tension without false positivity, leaving readers with genuine uncertainty about Vale's intentions and Nora's fate. The moral ambiguity requested in the prompt comes through clearly in Nora's compromised position and difficult choices. + Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
By the time JT caught up, his father was complaining about the weather. “Supposed to freeze tonight,” he said, though the sun was still up and sweat had darkened the band of his cap. “Ground’s too soft.” Mike grunted. He had a caribou quarter slung over one shoulder, blood soaking steadily through the canvas wrapping. They’d left the rest of the animal hung in a spruce to collect on the way back. JT could smell it whenever the wind shifted: warm iron under the clean rot of fallen needles. Neither of them mentioned the buck in the clearing. At supper, his father spoke about it. “Big one crossed ahead of us,” he said, reaching for the salt. “Too much brush for a shot.” Mike nodded over his plate. “Would’ve been a trophy.” JT looked up. Too much brush. He remembered open ground, pale grass, his father’s hand inches from the buck’s muzzle. He nearly said so. Instead he pushed a boiled potato around with his fork until it broke apart. Later, while Mike washed dishes, JT went out to bring in wood. The lodge stood in a shallow bowl of trees. Beyond the generator shed, the old trail ran north toward the abandoned hunting cabin. He had never seen the cabin himself. His grandfather had built it with two other men, back when the road stopped miles short of the lodge. In his father’s telling, it had rotted empty for thirty years. In Mike’s telling, hunters sometimes found a fire burning there, though no tracks ever led to the door. Once, when they were kids, Mike claimed there was something living inside that could make itself sound like anybody you knew. JT had believed that for an entire winter. The trail was barely visible now. At its entrance, a strip of red cloth hung from a branch. It stirred although the other branches were still. “JT.” He turned. His father stood on the porch, framed by yellow kitchen light. “Wood,” his father said. “Not a sightseeing trip.” JT picked up an armload and went inside. That night, he woke to the front door opening. He lay on the narrow bed and listened to boots cross the porch boards. A pause. Then the door clicked shut. From the bunk across the room, Mike breathed through his nose, slow and regular. JT checked his watch. Two-seventeen. Someone moved below, in the kitchen. A chair scraped. Water ran briefly from the tap. He thought of his father, who sometimes got up for a drink. Then he heard his father cough in the next room. JT held still. The floor downstairs creaked once more, under a weight that seemed to be waiting. In the morning, he found mud dried along the kitchen floorboards. Two narrow lines, spaced like hoofprints, ran from the front door to the table. There they turned, crossed one another, and went back. He crouched and touched one. The dirt came away powdery on his finger. “Track something in?” Mike asked behind him. JT stood too quickly. “Maybe.” Mike looked at the marks. “Could be your boots.” They could have been. His boots sat by the stove, their soles caked with yesterday’s mud. He did not turn them over. They set out after breakfast to retrieve the meat. His father took the lead, moving with more purpose than he had the day before. Twice JT thought he saw a shape between the trees, pacing them at a distance. Each time, it resolved into branches when he stopped. At the hanging spruce, the meat was gone. The rope remained, neatly coiled on the ground. No drag marks disturbed the moss. His father stared at the empty branch. “Bears?” Mike said. “Bear wouldn’t untie it.” Nobody said anything for a while. A jay called from deeper in the woods, then stopped mid-cry. His father bent and picked up the rope. “We’ll check the old cabin. Someone’s been out here.” JT felt the cold settle beneath his collar. They walked north. The trail narrowed until they had to turn sideways through young firs. His father followed it without hesitation. When JT asked if he remembered the way, his father said, “Of course.” The cabin appeared so suddenly JT almost walked into Mike. Its roof sagged in the middle, and moss covered the lower logs. A dark square of window faced them. Beside the door stood a chopping block with a fresh-looking split in it. His father saw it too. JT could tell by the way his shoulders rose. “Stay behind me,” he said. He crossed the clearing with his rifle ready. Mike followed. JT remained at the tree line, close enough to hear the door scrape open. Inside, his father called, “Hello?” No answer came. JT stepped onto the porch and looked past Mike’s shoulder. The cabin held a bunk, a stove, a table. Dust lay thick everywhere except on the table, where three places had been cleared in neat circles. In the middle stood a tin cup, full to the brim with dark water. His father lowered his rifle. He reached toward the cup. “Dad,” JT said. His father stopped. His hand hovered there a moment longer, then fell to his side. From the woods behind JT came the soft crack of a branch. Mike went to the doorway. “Something out there?” JT turned. At the edge of the clearing stood the buck. Its antlers were so broad they seemed to gather the dim spaces between the trees. It watched the cabin, not JT. His father brushed past him onto the porch. That bright, empty look had returned to his face. “It’s all right,” he said. JT did not know whom he meant. He grabbed his father’s sleeve. For an instant his father pulled gently against him, like a man trying not to wake someone. Then Mike slammed the cabin door. The sound cracked through the clearing. The buck flinched and vanished among the firs. JT’s father stumbled, catching himself against the porch rail. “What the hell?” he said. Mike stared at him. “You were walking toward it.” “No, I wasn’t.” They went back without checking the cabin again. JT walked last and kept looking over his shoulder, but the trail stayed empty. At the lodge, his father poured three stiff drinks. He set one in front of JT without comment. JT left it untouched. They ate canned stew and listened to the generator labor outside. Only after Mike went upstairs did JT remember the table. Three clear places in the dust. Three of them had entered the cabin. He remembered, too, the tin cup. He had seen his reflection in its water as he stood at the door: his small white face above the rim. Behind it, another face had been leaning close to his ear. He could not have missed it. He had noticed nothing at the time. JT sat at the table until the generator quit. In the silence afterward, he heard slow steps cross the porch. He watched the dark front window and tried to remember whether he had locked the door.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Stephen King-inspired surreal horror style requested. The author successfully maintains JT's perspective as an unreliable narrator caught between reality and supernatural dread. The writing captures the isolation and psychological ambiguity effectively, with JT consistently keeping his disturbing observations to himself. The atmospheric building is particularly well-executed. The progression from missing meat to the abandoned cabin creates mounting tension, and the detail of three cleared places in the dust with JT realizing he saw another face in the cup's reflection provides a genuinely unsettling payoff. The buck's recurring presence as a supernatural focal point works well as a central horror element. Character actions feel believable within the horror context. The father's inexplicable attraction to the buck, Mike's practical responses, and JT's fearful silence all ring true. The dialogue is naturalistic and serves the story effectively - the conversations about weather, the missing meat, and the terse exchanges at the cabin feel authentic to these characters. The prose style successfully emulates King's approach with grounded, clear sentences that build dread through accumulation of unsettling details rather than overwrought language. Descriptions like "warm iron under the clean rot of fallen needles" and "his small white face above the rim" are evocative without being purple. However, some elements feel slightly predictable within the horror genre - the abandoned cabin with fresh signs of use, the mysterious nighttime visitor, and the supernatural entity's influence over family members follow familiar patterns. The piece also relies heavily on atmosphere over character development, though this suits the horror genre and length constraints. The ending effectively maintains the ambiguous, dread-filled tone without false resolution. JT's realization about the reflection and his final fearful vigil provides appropriate closure while preserving the story's unsettling uncertainty. + Fantasy-humour: Hell is Other Demons — Score: 82.5
Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. 1000 words.
Model Output:
At seven in the morning, the hellhound was chewing the throne again. Lucifer stood in the doorway with his coffee and watched a length of black iron disappear between Cinder’s teeth. The throne had survived rebellions, sieges, and one unfortunate attempt to make it swivel. Its front left leg was losing to a dog who weighed less than a filing cabinet. “Leave it,” Lucifer said. Cinder’s tail struck the floor. He took another bite. Lucifer could have turned the iron to flame. He could have turned the dog to flame, though Cinder would have liked that. Instead he put his coffee down and fetched the rubber comet Lilith had bought him last week. Cinder spat out a bolt and accepted the comet. Lilith had come by three times that week. On Monday, to collect a book she did not take. On Wednesday, to ask whether he still had her pruning shears. Last night, to bring Cinder the comet. Each visit had lasted a little longer than it needed to, and each had ended before either of them said anything useful. The first appointment of the day was a dispute between the Department of Temptation and the Department of Consequences. Temptation had introduced a loyalty scheme. Consequences argued that it made repeat offenders difficult to sort. “You’re rewarding them for it,” said the director of Consequences. “We’re recognizing established customers,” said the director of Temptation. Lucifer approved the scheme on a trial basis, then required both departments to share the paperwork. Neither director looked pleased, which usually meant he had made the right decision. At ten, the throne room doors opened and Lilith walked in carrying a potted fern. Cinder abandoned the comet. He ran to her, dragging a small chain of drool from one fang. She scratched behind his ears and looked past him at the throne. “He’s still doing that?” “He waits until I’m in the room.” “He misses having someone here during the day.” “I’m here during the day.” Lilith examined the damaged leg. “Then perhaps he misses me.” Lucifer had no useful answer to that. She set the fern on a side table, where it immediately wilted. “It needs less light,” she said. “Everything does, eventually.” She gave him the look she used when he made a joke instead of answering a question. They went to the gardens together to find a place for the fern. The gardens had once been lava fields, but a former king with an interest in roses had insisted on soil. Most things still grew red. Lilith chose a sheltered patch by the wall and knelt to dig with her hands. Lucifer knelt beside her. From the far side of the wall came the steady sound of the mill, where souls who had been cruel to servants carried sacks too heavy to lift. It was an old punishment. Lilith brushed earth from a root and asked if the mill still ran through the night. “Only until eleven,” Lucifer said. “The neighbors complained.” “Good.” She pressed the soil down around the fern. They stayed there a moment, looking at it. At noon, Lucifer had a council meeting. Lilith meant to leave, but the stairwell was blocked by a procession of tax auditors carrying a newly deceased emperor. She came back upstairs and sat in the gallery while Lucifer heard petitions. One duke requested more screaming in his district. A second requested less, because the first duke’s district shared a wall with his bedroom. The kitchens reported a shortage of salt. Lucifer settled the noise complaint, signed an order for salt, and was halfway through a proposal for a new abyss when Cinder trotted in with an iron chair bracket in his mouth. The council went quiet. Lucifer held out his hand. Cinder dropped the bracket into it, pleased to have brought him something. Lilith came down from the gallery. “How much of the chair is left?” “Enough.” “That’s what you said last week.” “It was true last week.” She turned the throne slightly. One leg bent outward. Lucifer had been sitting with more care than usual and hoping no one noticed. “Have you called a smith?” she asked. “I’ve had a busy morning.” “You approved a loyalty scheme.” “That took longer than you’d think.” Cinder put his paws on Lilith’s knees. She pushed him down gently. “He needs a walk.” Lucifer glanced at the council. The duke was waiting to discuss screaming again. “He has the courtyard.” “That isn’t a walk.” The council members studied their papers. Lucifer adjourned the meeting and took Cinder out through the west gate. They walked along the River of Ash, where the ferryman was repainting his boat. Cinder sniffed every post and startled a pair of imps eating their lunch on the bank. Lilith told Lucifer about a house she had been considering on the border between realms. It had a kitchen large enough for a table and a bath that held hot water. “You should see it,” she said. “I could.” She looked at him. “I know you could.” He had spent the month imagining reasons to go there. None had survived the walk from his rooms to the lift. “I’d like to see it,” he said. Lilith bent to untangle Cinder’s lead from a railing. “All right.” By late afternoon, the smith had braced the throne. She advised Lucifer not to lean on its left arm until the new leg was ready. He thanked her and moved his next meeting to an ordinary chair. Lilith stayed for supper. They ate in the kitchen because Cinder had fallen asleep across the dining-room doorway. At nine, she washed the plates while Lucifer dried them. They argued briefly over where he kept the bowls. They had argued about the bowls when they lived together, too; he still kept them above the stove, and she still had to reach for them. When she was ready to go, Lucifer offered to show her the fern before the garden gates were locked. It looked much the same as it had that morning. “There’s tea upstairs,” he said. Lilith touched a leaf, then stood. “I can stay for tea.” Cinder woke at the sound of their footsteps. He followed them inside, carrying his rubber comet.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece successfully executes the prompt's requirements with considerable skill. The author creates a compelling "day in the life" narrative that effectively merges the grandiose mythology of Hell's rulers with mundane domestic concerns. The understated irony works particularly well - Lucifer dealing with departmental disputes over loyalty schemes while his hellhound destroys his throne creates exactly the kind of absurd juxtaposition requested. The Gaiman influence is evident in the matter-of-fact treatment of fantastical elements and the dry, observational tone. The prose is clean and economical, avoiding purple language while maintaining atmospheric richness. Details like "souls who had been cruel to servants carried sacks too heavy to lift" and "Most things still grew red" effectively establish the hellish setting without overwrought description. Character development is nuanced and believable. Lucifer emerges as lonely, somewhat passive, and struggling with relationship dynamics that feel genuinely human despite the supernatural context. Lilith's gradual warming - from brief visits to staying for tea - feels organic rather than forced. Their interactions carry authentic relationship tension, particularly in moments like the bowl placement argument that echoes their shared domestic history. The dark comedy lands consistently without becoming heavy-handed. The hellhound Cinder serves as an effective comedic and emotional anchor, his destruction of furniture paralleling the couple's fractured relationship while also providing moments of levity. The administrative aspects of Hell (noise complaints from torture districts, tax auditors) create humor through bureaucratic mundanity. However, the piece occasionally relies on convenient plot devices - Lilith's extended stay due to blocked stairs feels slightly contrived. Some dialogue exchanges, while functional, lack the spark that would elevate them from competent to memorable. The ending, while appropriate, doesn't quite achieve the emotional resonance that the careful buildup seems to promise. The pacing is generally strong, though certain transitions between scenes could be smoother. The piece maintains coherence throughout and avoids meandering, staying focused on the central relationship dynamic while incorporating the required fantastical elements effectively. + Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 81.6
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell at the Ludus Magnus rang before dawn, though the city had already begun to stir. Through the shutters came the groan of cart wheels on stone and the shouts of men unloading bread. Somewhere below our window, a donkey brayed with such conviction that Titus threw his sandal at the wall. “Your brother,” he said to me. I told him the animal had a finer singing voice. It was our oldest joke, and on mornings when we both laughed, I took it as a good omen. We ate in the courtyard: barley porridge, beans, and a heel of bread I saved for later. The air smelled of wet plaster and boiled grain. Beyond the roofline rose the upper arches of the amphitheatre, pale against a pink sky. Even from inside the school, we could hear the first vendors calling to those who had come early for seats. Titus sat beside me and rubbed his thumb over a crack in his cup. He had been born a citizen in Rome. His father had owned a shop that made lampstands until a fire took the shop and the lenders took what remained. Titus had signed himself into the school. I had arrived in chains after Trajan’s armies crossed the Danube. We ate the same porridge now, but when Titus spoke of leaving, he meant the street where he had grown up. I meant a village I could no longer picture without wondering who lived in it. The roster for the next day had not been posted. We watched the office door while we ate, as if the clerk might come out with it tucked under his arm. After breakfast, I went to the small shrine by the washbasins. Someone had left flowers for Hercules, already browning at the edges. My Mercury stood beside him, a little bronze figure with one wing broken from his cap. An older man called Marcellus had given him to me the winter before. Marcellus said Mercury watched over travellers and knew every road, including the ones no living person could walk. I touched the god’s cold foot. At first I had asked him to carry a message to my mother. Lately I had asked him to help me remember the sound of her voice. A new boy waited behind me with a basket of clean cloths. He had come from Dacia that summer and spoke Latin slowly, choosing each word before he let it go. He saw me at the shrine and asked, in our own language, whether Mercury was a god from home. “No,” I said. “But he gets about.” That made him smile. He asked if I had seen the column in Trajan’s new forum, where the emperor’s victories were carved in stone. I had seen it from a distance on an errand with a guard. Men stood beneath it pointing upward, trying to follow the little ranks of soldiers as they wound toward the top. The figures from my country had been too high for me to make out. “It’s very tall,” I told the boy. A horn sounded from the amphitheatre. He gathered his cloths and hurried away. Before noon, the steward sent Titus and me through the passage that joined the school to the amphitheatre. We were to collect oil from a storekeeper. The passage was cool and damp; water dripped steadily somewhere beyond the lamps. At its far end, daylight fell across the floor, and with it came a rush of voices. The morning’s entertainments had begun. We waited by a service gate while the storekeeper counted jars. Men passed us carrying benches, baskets of rushes, a cage covered in heavy cloth. A seller slipped through after them, hoping to reach the attendants with his tray of honey cakes. He offered me one at twice the street price. When I refused, he lowered it to a price I could afford. I bought it and split it with Titus. From where we stood, I could see people moving along the upper walks, searching for their places. Down in the city, citizens could collect grain because their names appeared on a register. In the amphitheatre, every rank had its entrance and its seats. Titus knew which gate his father had once used, back when he could afford to bring his sons. He pointed it out to me. Then he looked away and licked honey from his thumb. The storekeeper returned with three jars instead of four. He and our steward argued over a wax tablet while Titus held the empty carrying pole. The seller had gone by then. I ate the last crumb of cake from my palm and watched a pair of sparrows hopping under a bench. They had found more to eat here than we had. On our way back, we passed the office. The clerk had pinned up the roster. Titus stopped so abruptly that one of the jars knocked against his leg. My name was there for the next day. His was not. I read the list twice, though I had understood it the first time. Titus reached past me and straightened the tablet, which hung crooked from its nail. Then he put his hand on my shoulder. He left it there until someone behind us asked to see. Back in the courtyard, the sun had warmed the washbasin. I poured water over my hands, rubbing away a smear of oil from the jar. The Dacian boy came to take the cloths from the line. He glanced at me, but neither of us mentioned the roster. We spoke instead about whether the clouds gathering over the eastern roofs meant rain. I went to the shrine once more before supper. Mercury’s broken wing had caught a little sunlight. I gave him the crust I had saved from breakfast, setting it where the ants would find it. Then I sat beside Titus and watched the clouds.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical competence and atmospheric writing within the historical fiction genre. The author successfully creates an immersive Roman setting through carefully chosen sensory details - the sound of cart wheels on stone, the smell of wet plaster and boiled grain, and the visual of the amphitheatre's arches against a pink sky. The first-person narration maintains consistency throughout, and the voice feels authentic to the character and period. The characterization is particularly well-handled. The protagonist emerges as a complex figure - a Dacian captive who has adapted to Roman life while retaining connections to his homeland. His relationship with Titus provides emotional depth without sentimentality, and their different backgrounds (citizen versus captive) illuminate the social stratification of Roman society. The brief interaction with the younger Dacian boy adds another layer, showing how the protagonist has become a bridge between worlds. The piece effectively incorporates historical and social context without heavy-handedness. References to Trajan's column, the grain dole, and the amphitheatre's seating arrangements feel natural rather than forced exposition. The contrast between citizen privileges and gladiator status is woven throughout rather than explicitly stated. The writing demonstrates restraint and subtlety. The revelation that the protagonist's name appears on the roster - meaning he will fight the next day - is handled with understated tension. The emotional weight comes through small gestures: Titus straightening the crooked tablet, his hand on the protagonist's shoulder, their conversation about clouds instead of the obvious topic. However, the piece occasionally relies on somewhat predictable elements - the shrine visits, the honey cake sharing, the ominous roster posting. While these work within the narrative, they don't surprise or challenge expectations significantly. The ending, while tonally consistent, doesn't provide particular insight or revelation beyond the established mood. The prose is clean and readable, though it doesn't reach exceptional heights of literary achievement. Some descriptions, while competent, remain fairly standard ("pale against a pink sky," "cool and damp"). The dialogue, though limited, feels natural and serves character development well. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 81.3
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**The Lighthouse Keeper** **Bell Rock, 4 April 1936** Mam, We reached the rock before breakfast. From the boat it looked too small to hold a lighthouse, never mind three men. At high water there’s nothing outside the walls but sea. Mr Forsyth showed me the lamps and the winding gear. There’s enough work here to keep my hands occupied. When the weather clears, I can make out the red cliffs by Arbroath. I thought you’d like to know I can see home from my window. I’ve put my first wages in the post. Your Alec **Arbroath, 9 April 1936** Alec, I can see the light from the upstairs landing if I lean past Mrs Donnelly’s washing. Don’t tell her. She’ll charge me for the view. Your wages arrived. I’ve paid the coal man and put the rest aside, so stop counting pennies on my account. Eat a proper dinner even if Mr Forsyth makes one sound like an extravagance. Mrs Donnelly says the harbour is quiet without your opinions on everyone’s ropes. Love, Mam **Bell Rock, 21 June 1936** Mam, Mr Forsyth doesn’t talk much. Neither does Neil, unless he’s explaining why Mr Forsyth is wrong. I thought I’d welcome the peace after the docks. Yesterday I caught myself telling the kettle that Neil had left the lid off the flour tin. I was halfway through the argument before I noticed. It’s the same few rooms every day, and the same sound at the windows, though the sea never does quite the same thing twice. Please send the paper when you’re finished with it. I even miss the adverts. Alec **Arbroath, 26 June 1936** Alec, The paper is enclosed, including three advertisements for sensible boots. Take the hint. I’ve been mending Mrs Donnelly’s curtains. She wanted them shortened by two inches and stood over me with a ruler, as if I’d never held a needle. I charged her an extra sixpence. You needn’t worry about her finding out; she knows. You could ask Neil about his people. An argument over flour might get you through a morning, but there must be more to the man. Mam **Bell Rock, 3 September 1936** Mam, Neil has two girls. The youngest calls every boat a ferry and asks when he’s coming home on it. He showed me her drawing. She’d given the lighthouse four chimneys, so it was a poor likeness, but he’s pinned it over his bunk. I told him about your curtains and he laughed hard enough to wake Forsyth. That was good. The relief boat was turned back twice this week. I’ve run out of clean shirts and am beginning to think of the shore as a place I invented. Alec **Arbroath, 11 September 1936** Alec, I’ve sent shirts. I washed them, but if they smell damp by the time they reach you, don’t blame me. I’ve taken a morning at the school, helping the smaller children with their sums. One boy insists that if he has six apples he’ll eat them before anyone can subtract two. I’ve told him he’ll do well in the fish trade. You sounded more like yourself writing about Neil. Keep doing that, even when you don’t feel inclined. Love, Mam **Bell Rock, 18 December 1936** Mam, It gets dark before I’ve properly begun the day. We clean, check, wind, make meals, and begin again. I know each scrape on the stair. One night I lay awake waiting for a footstep I knew would come; it was only Forsyth going up to his watch. I had shore leave last month and didn’t come to Arbroath. I stood in Montrose among people and found I couldn’t think what to say to any of them. I’m sorry. I told you the boat had been delayed because it was easier than explaining that. Alec **Arbroath, 23 December 1936** Alec, I was angry about the visit, not because you owed me one but because I knew you’d been ashore. Neil wrote his wife from Montrose, and she met me at the butcher’s. You mustn’t ask me to pretend along with you. I’m sorry it has become so hard. When your dad died, I sometimes went all day without speaking because I thought I ought to be managing. It didn’t make me manage better. Tell Forsyth you need more time ashore. Tell me the truth, even if it’s only that you’ve had a bad day. Mam **Bell Rock, 8 January 1937** Mam, I’ve read your letter six times. On Tuesday my watch ended and I sat on the stair instead of going to bed. I couldn’t bear the thought of waking up to do the same things. Forsyth found me there. I said I was tired. He said he could see that. We kept the light as we should. I don’t want you frightened about that. I am frightened by how little I’ve cared about anything else. I’ll speak to him properly tonight. Alec **Arbroath, 13 January 1937** Alec, I am frightened, and I’m glad you told me. Speak to Forsyth, then write and tell me what he said. If you need to leave the rock, you can. Your wages help, but I have the school mornings and more sewing than I want. I would rather complain to you about money than wonder how you are while you say nothing. I’ve put a photograph in with this. It was taken outside the school. I’m in the back row because the wee ones kept pulling faces when I stood beside them. Love, Mam **Bell Rock, 28 January 1937** Mam, Forsyth listened. He said he’d noticed I was sleeping badly and should have asked sooner. Neil took my watch that afternoon so I could rest. I didn’t sleep, but we played cards after supper, and I lost four games without minding much. Forsyth has written to the superintendent about a transfer. There may be a vacancy at Scurdie Ness in spring. I’d still be keeping a light, and I could walk into Montrose when my shift was done. Your photograph is beside Neil’s daughter’s drawing. The boy in front looks ready to eat everyone’s apples. Alec **Arbroath, 2 February 1937** Alec, That boy is the very one. He came to school with two apples yesterday and gave one away, though I had made no such calculation for him. I’ve had to change my opinion of his prospects. I’m pleased Forsyth listened. I wish you’d told him earlier, but then I wish I’d asked you more plainly when you were home. We can both do better at that. Come on your next leave. We needn’t make a grand occasion of it. I’ll get haddock and you can tell me whether I’ve cooked it properly. Mam **Scurdie Ness, 17 May 1937** Mam, I got here on Monday. There’s a road to the lighthouse, and yesterday I walked into Montrose for a loaf I didn’t need. I asked the baker which way was shortest coming back and took the longer way he pointed out. It went past the river. The work is familiar. I was glad of that when I came on watch. I still have bad mornings, but now I can say so, and after my shift I can go somewhere. Neil wrote to say Forsyth has started marking the cards before anyone deals. They both send regards. I’ll come down on Sunday. Buy the haddock; I won’t criticise it. Your Alec
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This epistolary narrative successfully fulfills most of the prompt requirements while delivering a genuinely moving story about isolation, mental health, and family bonds. The author demonstrates strong technical control over the letter format, creating two distinct voices that feel authentic to their characters and time period. The Scottish working-class voice is handled with restraint and authenticity. Rather than relying on heavy dialect or stereotypical expressions, the author captures the character through sentence structure, word choice, and cultural details. Alec's voice feels genuinely Scottish without becoming caricature, and his mother's voice complements his perfectly - practical, loving, and perceptive. The gradual revelation of Alec's deteriorating mental state is skillfully managed. The progression from initial optimism through growing isolation to near-breakdown feels organic and believable. The author shows rather than tells this decline through concrete details: talking to the kettle, avoiding shore leave, sitting on stairs unable to face another day. These moments carry genuine emotional weight. The mother emerges as a fully realized character despite the constraints of the format. Her practicality ("I charged her an extra sixpence"), her perceptiveness about her son's condition, and her firm but loving approach to his deception create a three-dimensional person. The relationship between mother and son feels lived-in and real. The historical setting is well-researched and convincingly rendered. Details like the Bell Rock lighthouse, the relief boats, and the social context feel authentic without overwhelming the personal story. The author demonstrates good period knowledge while keeping focus on character. The emotional climax builds naturally from Alec's confession of his mental state through to the resolution. The transformation feels earned because it involves both personal honesty and practical change - Forsyth's understanding, the transfer to a less isolated posting, and improved communication with his mother. However, the piece has some limitations. While competently executed, it doesn't take significant creative risks or offer particularly surprising insights into its themes. The trajectory from isolation to recovery, while well-handled, follows a fairly predictable path. Some opportunities for deeper complexity are missed - we learn little about what specifically draws Alec to lighthouse keeping, or about his father's death beyond brief mention. The prose is clean and effective but rarely rises to memorable heights. It serves the story well without achieving particular elegance or beauty. The ending, while satisfying, perhaps resolves things a bit too neatly - the transfer comes through conveniently, and Alec's recovery seems to proceed smoothly. The piece succeeds as a solid, emotionally engaging story that handles its difficult subject matter with sensitivity and skill, even if it doesn't reach the heights of truly exceptional creative writing. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 83.8
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The restaurant has a QR-code menu taped to every table, which means I spend the first three minutes of my first date trying not to inspect the URL. I used to think this made me useful. It does, sometimes. Now it mostly means I notice the loose floor tile by the hostess stand, the laptop open behind the counter, and the way a stranger’s name lights up on a phone when they leave it faceup beside their drink. None of these things is my business. That sentence is less a belief than a practice. My date arrives wearing a raincoat and an expression that says the weather has personally disappointed her. “Sorry,” she says. “The bus gave up.” Her name is Maya. We met through an app that thinks loving museums and hating cilantro constitutes compatibility. In person, she has bright eyes, damp hair, and an enamel pin shaped like a tiny green tree. I glance at it, then away. Do not inventory the woman. Talk to her. We order noodles. She tells me about the ceramics studio where she works, how the kiln has been temperamental all week. I tell her I do freelance security work, which is true and sounds better than *I get paid to worry professionally*. She doesn’t ask for a story about a data breach. Instead, she asks whether I ever make anything with my hands. “Bad coffee,” I say. She laughs. I feel my shoulders lower. Then she says she painted a mug last month with the Selesnya symbol on it. I nearly knock over my water. “You play Magic?” “Commander, mostly. And badly.” There are people who say *badly* because they want you to argue. Maya says it with obvious affection for her own terrible decisions. She describes a deck built around making too many tokens and forgetting what half of them do. I admit I once spent an entire Saturday tuning a graveyard deck only to discover my friends had all added graveyard hate. “That’s what you get,” she says, “for treating the dead like a resource.” “I thought they’d want to feel included.” Somewhere between the appetizers and an argument about whether a dragon should be allowed in every deck, I stop counting exits. The restaurant becomes a restaurant. The candle on the table is a candle, not an unattended flame near a paper menu. Maya leans forward when I speak. I do the same. Her phone buzzes. “My sister,” she says, picking it up. “She’s watching Pickle.” I try not to read the screen. I learn, despite myself, that Pickle is a dog, that Maya’s sister is named Lena, and that Maya’s lock screen shows a little girl with enormous glasses standing beside a pony. Maya smiles at the photo before unlocking her phone. Her finger draws the simplest possible shape across the pattern grid. My brain supplies an objection so fast it feels like a reflex. No, not a reflex. A reflex is blinking at a sudden light. This is something I’ve practiced for years, and practice can be interrupted. I could interrupt it now. “That’s a pretty easy pattern to guess,” I say. Maya’s finger stops. So does the nice, warm current carrying the evening along. She puts the phone down. “Oh.” I know that *oh*. It is the sound of someone deciding whether they feel embarrassed or irritated, and finding room for both. “I’m sorry,” I say. “You were watching me unlock my phone?” “No. I mean, yes. I saw it. I wasn’t trying to.” A poor distinction, even if it’s true. Maya folds her napkin once, very neatly. “And you thought I should know?” “I thought—” I thought warning her would make me helpful. I thought being right would excuse saying it. “I didn’t think enough.” She looks at me for a moment. Her phone buzzes again, and she turns it facedown without checking it. Across the table sits a person who has spent the evening telling me things freely: that her sister lives two streets over, that Pickle came from the same shelter as the pony in the photo, that her first job was at her dad’s garden center in Ashland. She mentioned her childhood best friend while explaining how she got into Magic. I remember all of it. I remember names I have no reason to retain. A security question could ask for any one of them. I could point that out, too. Give her a brisk little lecture on what strangers can piece together. I can already hear myself making it worse. “I notice things,” I say. “It’s my job, and I’m bad at leaving it at work. That’s an explanation, not a defense.” She lets the napkin go. “Did you look at anything else?” The question hurts, which seems fair. “I caught your sister’s name and your dog’s. Your phone was right there, and I should have looked away.” I resist listing the other details. She already knows what she told me; repeating them now would only prove I kept count. “Okay,” she says. Not forgiveness. A receipt for the answer. The server arrives with our noodles. We both thank him with extravagant gratitude. For a while, we eat. Mine are too hot. I am grateful for a problem I can solve by waiting. “I know you meant well,” Maya says eventually. “But it felt like you were grading me.” “I was,” I say. “For about half a second. I’m sorry.” She tilts her head. “Is this what dating you is like? Surprise audit over dinner?” “No. Or it shouldn’t be.” I take a breath. “If we keep talking, I’ll try to remember I’m here as myself, not as a consultant.” “And if I ask for phone advice?” “I can give it. Then I have to stop when you want me to.” Her mouth lifts at one corner. “That sounds like a challenge.” “It may be the hardest one I’ve had this week.” She laughs, quietly, and takes another bite. A few minutes later she tells me her token deck has never won a game against Lena’s. I ask what Lena plays. Maya says blue-black, naturally, because sisters are obligated to be villains. I can feel the evening finding its way back, though more carefully now. She has my attention. I have to learn that attention alone isn’t always a gift; it matters what I do with it. When the bill comes, Maya reaches for it before I can. “I’ll get my half,” she says. I let her. Outside, the rain has stopped. We stand under the restaurant awning, close enough that I can see the little green tree on her coat again. “Want to play Commander sometime?” she asks. I try not to treat the question as a test. “Yeah. I’d like that.” “Good,” she says. “I’m going to make you lose to the tokens.” I hope she does.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and adherence to the prompt's specific requirements. The first-person narrative successfully captures the mindset of a reformed hacker who compulsively notices vulnerabilities, from QR code URLs to loose floor tiles to insecure phone patterns. The internal monologue format is maintained throughout, creating an intimate window into the protagonist's thought processes. The characterization is particularly well-handled. The protagonist feels authentic - their struggle between professional instincts and personal connection is believable and relatable. Maya emerges as a fully realized person rather than a plot device, with specific details about her ceramics work, her family, and her Magic: The Gathering hobby that feel natural rather than forced. The shared nerd fandom provides genuine chemistry and serves as an effective bridge between the characters. The central conflict - the protagonist's inability to resist commenting on Maya's insecure phone pattern - feels organic to the character and creates realistic tension. The fallout is handled with emotional intelligence; Maya's reaction ("Oh") and subsequent responses feel genuine rather than melodramatic. The protagonist's self-awareness about their mistake and their attempt to explain without excusing shows character depth. The prose is clean and efficient, with moments of genuine wit ("I get paid to worry professionally") and insightful observations ("practice can be interrupted"). The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining engaging descriptive elements. The pacing moves naturally from setup through conflict to tentative resolution. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - not overly optimistic but suggesting possibility. The protagonist has learned something about boundaries and attention, while Maya shows both appropriate caution and willingness to continue. The final exchange about Magic feels earned rather than forced. Minor weaknesses include some moments where the internal monologue becomes slightly expository, and a few instances where the hacker mindset observations feel somewhat mechanical rather than fully integrated into the character's psychology. However, these are relatively minor issues in an otherwise well-executed piece. + First-person unique perspective: Overthinking It — Score: 87.5
Prompt:
Overthinking It Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The projector squeaks every time Ms. Alvarez flips to a new slide. Not a normal electronic beep. An actual squeak, like a sneaker dragged across a gym floor. Squeak. **BUILD A MODEL ECOSYSTEM.** Squeak. **GROUPS OF TWO.** Squeak. **DUE NEXT FRIDAY.** If she keeps clicking, maybe the projector will announce the exact second I’m supposed to speak. “Lena, you’re with Miles,” Ms. Alvarez says. My pencil stops halfway through writing *producers, consumers, decomposers*. Miles sits two tables over, drawing tiny stars in the corner of his notebook. I have liked him since October, when he lent me a ruler without making a joke about how I’d forgotten mine. That sounds like a very low standard for liking someone. I know. He also asks questions in class that are actually questions, not speeches disguised as questions, and he laughs with his whole face. I get up. Am I getting up too fast? Normal people don’t evaluate the speed at which they stand. Unfortunately, knowing this does not make me one of them. Miles pulls out the chair beside him. “Hey.” “Hey,” I say. Excellent. A complete sentence would have been showy. Ms. Alvarez gives us a sheet with spaces for our ecosystem, materials, and division of work. I can explain how energy moves through a food web. I can explain why a closed terrarium isn’t really closed if sunlight can enter it. In my head, I can explain all of this while casually asking Miles what he thinks and somehow sounding like a person who has conversations every day. Out loud, I say, “Um.” He looks up. Not impatiently. Just because I made a sound. Now I have to finish it. “Do you—” I glance at the worksheet. “Have an ecosystem?” A terrible question. Everyone has an ecosystem. We are currently inside several. Miles studies the list. “I was thinking pond, maybe. But I’m open to other ideas.” “I like ponds,” I say. I do like ponds. This is the problem with being nervous: even the truth sounds made up. Squeak. Ms. Alvarez changes to a slide showing an example model with blue plastic wrap for water. Miles turns toward the screen, and I use the three seconds to arrange my face. Interested, but not intensely interested. Friendly, but not like I’ve spent four months noticing what he does with his hands when he’s trying to remember an answer. I should contribute something useful. *A pond would let us show interactions at different levels: algae, insects, fish, birds.* Clear. Relevant. Eleven words, depending on whether “different levels” counts as two, which it does. “We could do algae,” I say. “Yeah,” Miles says. “And dragonflies?” “Yes.” My brain supplies *Dragonfly nymphs are predators, which would make the underwater part more interesting.* My mouth supplies nothing. He writes **POND** at the top of the sheet, in letters that lean slightly right. We need to divide the work. I should offer to build the model. No, if I offer too quickly, he’ll think I’m desperate to impress him. If I don’t offer, he’ll think I expect him to do everything. If I say I’m good at drawing, he might ask to see my sketchbook, and the last four pages contain the same sneaker I kept trying to draw because it was on his foot. “Are you okay doing the research?” he asks. “I can bring stuff for the model.” “Yes. I mean, I can bring stuff too. Not that I have pond stuff at my house. I have cardboard.” My cheeks go hot. Cardboard is normal. Most people have cardboard. I have somehow said it as though it’s a secret. Miles smiles. “Cardboard would help.” I look at the worksheet. If I look at him now, I might smile too much. There is an amount of smiling that says *pleasant classmate*, and another amount that says *I know you were absent the Tuesday before winter break*. I cannot reliably locate the boundary. Ms. Alvarez walks by. “Good start. Think about what lives below the surface, too.” “Dragonfly nymphs,” I say, much too loudly. She nods. “Perfect.” Miles turns to me. “That’s what I was trying to remember they’re called.” “Oh.” I could say, *They look completely different from adult dragonflies.* I could ask if he’s ever found one in a pond. I could make a joke about how weird it is that something can live underwater and then just grow wings. I press my thumbnail into the side of my finger instead. It leaves a little crescent. Squeak. The next slide is a checklist. Ms. Alvarez reads it aloud while everyone starts talking over her. Around us, people trade ideas without first inspecting every possible meaning. I watch a girl across the room lean over her partner’s page and say, “That’s ugly,” then laugh, and her partner laughs too. I would need a week to recover from either side of that conversation. Miles taps the pencil against our worksheet. “You were going to say something?” Was I? I probably was. My mouth had opened while the thought about dragonflies was passing through. “I was thinking,” I say. I stop. That much is obvious. He waits. I notice he isn’t filling the silence for me, which makes it harder, but also better. “Dragonfly nymphs could go underwater in the model,” I say. “Like, below a clear layer. Since people usually only think of the ones with wings.” “That’s cool.” He sketches a line across the page. “Could we use plastic from a container?” I have three answers ready. *Yes, provided it’s transparent enough to see through.* Too formal. *Totally, that would look awesome.* Too enthusiastic. *Sure.* Too little. “Yeah,” I say. “I think so.” He adds a note: **CLEAR PLASTIC—LENA?** Seeing my name on the page beside his makes me briefly forget how to hold my pencil. I take the sheet and write **check recycling bin** underneath. My handwriting is almost normal. The bell rings before we finish. Miles asks if we should compare research tomorrow. I say yes without rehearsing it first. The word comes out small, but it comes out on time. As I pack up, I replay the entire conversation. The cardboard comment. The loud nymphs. Every pause. I’ll probably replay it on the bus and again while brushing my teeth. Then Miles points at my note. “I like that you thought of putting something below the water.” “I like your idea about the plastic,” I tell him. It sounds a little stiff. He smiles anyway. Maybe tomorrow I’ll tell him the thing about dragonflies growing wings. I can practice it tonight. Or I can remember that I already knew what I wanted to say today, and eventually I said it.

Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The battery icon is red when I pick up my phone. Four percent. Mara’s last message is still open: *See you at seven. I’m looking forward to it.* I read it the way I read everything from her now, as if there’s another message underneath and I might expose it by pressing hard enough. *Looking forward to it* is good. She chose those words. On Tuesday she sent only a heart when I told her about my day, and yesterday she didn’t answer for six hours. Before we slept together, six hours meant she was busy. Now it means I made things strange. Or she regrets it. Or she doesn’t, but she knows I do, and she’s giving me room to admit it first. I stand in front of my closet with one shoe on. In the version of tonight that keeps playing in my head, Mara says, “I love you, but this is too much.” She will say it gently, because she is gentle, which will make it worse. I’ll say, “You could have told me sooner.” She’ll say she tried. I’ll ask when. I have already prepared examples of every time she didn’t: Tuesday’s heart, yesterday’s silence, the two times last week she called me her friend after kissing me. She called me her friend because I am her friend. I know that. I also know exactly how I’ll bring it up. My phone buzzes. The screen lights my hands: *I’m leaving now. Want me to grab you a coffee?* Three percent. She’s offering me coffee because she remembers I like coffee. She’s offering because she wants an easy thing to do with her hands while she tells me we should go back to how we were. I type *Yes please*, delete it, type *You don’t have to*, delete that. If I ask for something, will it feel like a demand? If I say no, will she think I’m sulking? *Yes please. The usual if they have it.* Her reply comes at once. *Of course.* Of course. Two words I could live in. Two words I could spend all evening inspecting for cracks. I plug in my phone while I change my shirt. The charger has to sit at an angle to work, so I keep looking over to check for the little lightning bolt. Five percent. Six. My therapist has a name for what I’m doing when I turn a missed message into a complete conversation. I have a name too: preparation. If I imagine the hurt properly, maybe it won’t take me by surprise. That has never worked. I put on my coat anyway, rehearsing. At the café, Mara is already at a table by the window. There are two cups in front of her. She smiles when she sees me—not a polite smile, not one I have to earn by being easy tonight. She lifts my cup and waves it a little, as if she’s pleased to have got something right. My phone says eight percent. I put it facedown on the table. She asks about the meeting I was nervous about this morning. She remembers its name and the person I said would be difficult. While I tell her, she listens. No glances at the door. No practiced expression of patience. She laughs at the part where I spill water on my notes, then stops and asks, “Was that awful?” “No. I mean, yes. But it’s funny now.” She touches my wrist. Her hand is warm. For one whole breath I believe her smile and her hand and the coffee she brought me. My chest opens so suddenly it almost hurts. I want to tell her how much I needed this, but then she’ll know how easily she can undo me. I turn my cup between my palms and say the meeting went fine. She asks if I want to walk after coffee. I do. She tells me about her week: a deadline, her sister visiting, a leak in the ceiling above her kitchen sink. I hear the reasons her messages were short. I also hear how carefully she is giving me reasons. Perhaps she can tell I’ve been counting the hours. Outside, the wind is cold enough that she tucks her hand through my arm. I have spent two days growing angry at her for pulling away. I had been planning to bring up those two times she called me her friend. Now I lean toward her, relieved, and feel foolish about the anger. Then I feel angry that I’m so relieved. She was distant. I noticed it. I’m allowed to have noticed it. We stop at the crossing. She says, “I’m sorry I’ve been hard to reach. I wanted to see you when I could actually be here.” The green man appears. I don’t move. This is the part I rehearsed, except she hasn’t asked for distance. She has come out in the cold, bought my coffee, put her hand through my arm. I could ask her what she means. I could also turn her apology into evidence and demand to know how long she knew I was worrying. Both responses are ready. “I missed you,” I say. “I missed you too.” She waits for me to step off the curb with her. I do. Halfway across, I let myself believe she means it. By the other side, I’m wondering whether she said it because I needed to hear it. My phone buzzes in my pocket. I don’t take it out. It’s probably the battery warning. Mara’s arm is still linked with mine, and I’m trying to pay attention to the weight of it.
