Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Polymerase Chain Reaction The solar panels had been meant for a billboard. Their glass was crazed with old hail scars, and every time a cloud crossed the sun, the lab lights browned to amber. Mara watched the voltage needle twitch. On the bench beneath it, a salvaged medical thermocycler clicked and went quiet. “Don’t you dare,” she told it. The machine clicked again. She hit the casing with the heel of her hand, and it resumed its low, uneven hum. Outside the greenhouse walls, Saint Acre was planting its last reliable seed. That was how the companies had made it: fruit that fed you, seed that disappointed you. The first harvest was abundant enough to make the purchase feel wise. The next grew pale, if it grew at all. Farmers had called it bad luck until the corporate warehouses started selling replacement packets at triple the price. Then the trucks stopped coming. Mara held a strip of clear film to the light. Three bands appeared, faint as ghosts. She compared them to the photograph taped above her bench: what the crop had been designed to carry, and what its children had lost. “Still falling apart?” someone asked. Tav stood in the doorway in a motorcycle helmet with no visor. He was Saint Acre’s courier, though nobody called it that when he brought in black-market parcels. There was rain on his shoulders and a sealed red tube in his hand. Mara set down the film. “What did you trade?” “My winning personality.” “Tav.” “Two coils of copper and the south pump’s spare bearing. The broker wouldn’t take promises.” Mara looked toward the greenhouse. Without that bearing, the pump would fail for good the next time grit reached its housing. Tav put the tube on the bench. “Open it.” Inside was a contract printed on flexible foil, and beneath it a thumb-sized vial in a padded sleeve. The vial’s label bore the crown-and-root logo of Vesper Agricultural: a company that had once supplied half the continent’s grain and had never supplied anything for free. Mara read the terms twice. The broker would provide an intact ancestral line of Vesper’s drought-resistant millet. In return, Mara would use it to make a crop that bred true—one that passed its engineered traits to its seed. At first harvest, Saint Acre would surrender every viable second-generation seed to the broker. The settlement could keep the grain. “No,” she said. “You haven’t looked at the vial.” “I read the contract.” “There’s an amendment.” Tav tapped the bottom of the foil. Mara read it. If she failed, the broker took the greenhouse. She laughed once, without humor. “You signed this?” “The council signed it. I carried it.” From the doorway came a cough so hard it bent Tav double. When he straightened, a fine red thread ran from his nose. Mara handed him a rag. “You took another dose.” “The fever came back.” Three winters earlier, Mara had coaxed a salvaged treatment into Tav’s bloodstream. It had stopped a lung infection that should have killed him. Since then, his bones knitted quickly and the old scars on his hands had faded. He could carry twice what he used to. He also ran fevers in warm weather and bled whenever the air turned dry. They had no way to ask his body what else it was doing. “You could have come to me,” she said. “You were here.” He gestured at the lab: the old thermocycler tethered to the billboard panels, a centrifuge made from a fan motor, reagent bottles cradled in socks to keep them warm. A child’s toy microscope sat beside a cracked corporate reader that accepted batteries only if its lid was held shut with wire. Mara lived among machines that needed constant coaxing. Tav had stopped wanting to be one more thing she had to fix. The voltage needle dipped. The thermocycler went dark. Mara swore and hurried outside to turn the panel toward a slit of sun. Beyond the lab, Saint Acre’s terraces climbed the slope in strips of green and brown. Families were pressing seed into soil with their thumbs. At the far edge of the settlement stood the old Vesper depot, its loading doors welded shut. Ten years ago, trucks had arrived there every spring. The council had stripped the depot for parts after the famine, but no one had taken down the logo. It still faced the fields. When Mara returned, Tav had unfolded the contract to its signature panel. Six council marks sat there, including her mother’s. “They signed because the bins are empty,” he said. “They signed away the harvest before it exists.” Mara lifted the vial from its sleeve. Whatever was inside had crossed a ruined country in a courier’s pocket. It might be dead already. It might be a fraud. Under the microscope, the sample showed traces of what the broker claimed to have found. Mara worked through the afternoon, using fragments from her own failing millet and the material from the vial. The panel’s voltage rose and fell. Each time it dropped, she waited beside the machine, afraid to touch it and afraid not to. By dusk, she had a result. It was thin, and it was incomplete, but a portion of the missing inheritance was there. The crop might hold it long enough to produce seed. She could not know more until something grew. Tav read her face. “It worked?” “It gave us a chance.” He leaned against the doorframe. “The broker comes tomorrow.” “They’ll bring carts.” “Yes.” “For seed we don’t have yet.” “They can afford to wait.” Mara folded the contract and held it over the alcohol lamp. Tav caught her wrist. “Burning it won’t stop them.” “No.” She lowered the foil. “But I’m not going to let the council think this is settled.” “They saw the terms.” “Did they see this?” She pointed to a clause buried in the lower margin. The broker could inspect the fields and take a sample from every plant before harvest. Any line it judged promising became its property at once. Tav read it, then read it again. “I missed that.” “So did they, I think.” Outside, the last light caught the depot logo. Mara thought of the farmers who had returned there year after year, paying for seed because the seed they saved would not feed their children. The broker’s contract offered the same bargain with one season’s mercy. She put the vial back in its sleeve and picked up the promising sample. “What are you doing?” Tav asked. “Showing the council what we have. And what they signed.” “They might still choose the contract.” “They might.” Mara switched off the lamp. “But they’ll choose it knowing which part of the harvest the broker wants.” The lab went dark except for the thermocycler’s small green light. This time, when the clouds passed over the panels, it stayed on.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This biopunk chapter successfully establishes a compelling post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering with built-in obsolescence has created a desperate survival scenario. The author demonstrates strong world-building through specific details like the jury-rigged lab equipment (thermocycler powered by salvaged billboard solar panels, centrifuge made from a fan motor) and the physical toll of genetic modifications (Tav's bleeding, fevers, but also enhanced healing and strength). The central black market contract provides effective narrative tension, with the settlement risking their greenhouse for potentially viable seeds. The author skillfully reveals the contract's predatory nature through Mara's discovery of the buried clause that allows the broker to claim promising plant lines before harvest - a clever parallel to the original corporate seed scam. Character development is nuanced, particularly Mara's expertise contrasted with her resource limitations, and Tav's complex relationship with his genetic modifications. Their dialogue feels natural and reveals character efficiently. The relationship dynamics suggest history and mutual care without over-explanation. The prose maintains an appropriately gritty, technical tone that suits the biopunk genre. Scientific details feel authentic without becoming overly technical. The imagery of the failing equipment, the settlement's terraces, and the abandoned Vesper depot creates a vivid sense of place. However, the chapter suffers from some pacing issues in the middle section where technical processes slow momentum. The ending, while thematically appropriate, feels somewhat predictable - the discovery of the hidden contract clause and Mara's decision to inform the council follows expected beats. The emotional stakes, while present, could be heightened further to create more urgency around the settlement's desperation. The writing occasionally tells rather than shows, particularly regarding the historical context of corporate seed manipulation. Some transitions between scenes feel abrupt, and certain character motivations could be more deeply explored.
